articles.title: Trump ‘border czar’ denies that Milo Yiannopoulos was deported for political reasons
articles.summary:
Tom Homan says rightwing influencer overstayed visitor visa after receiving final order of removal

The White House “border czar,” Tom Homan, denied on Sunday that the British far-right…

blocks.text: The White House “border czar,” Tom Homan, denied on Sunday that the British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was deported just a day after being arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for political reasons.

Homan said it was his understanding that Yiannopoulos, 41, had overstayed what he believed to be a visitor visa, had not appeared at an immigration hearing and was issued a final order of removal on 22 July.

“He didn’t show up,” Homan told CNN’s State of the Union. “The judge ordered him deported. So, once ICE gets an order of deportation from a federal judge, their job is to execute that order, and that’s what they did.”
He added: “He had his due process, ordered removed by a federal judge, and ICE removed him. It’s that simple.”

Yiannopoulos’s removal one day after his arrest, when many others who have been deported had first endured lengthy detention center incarcerations, has prompted questions about whether he received preferential treatment in that respect. Homan said the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, was trying to speed up the deportation process.

“Once a judge orders them out, rather than being in detention, waiting for travel documents and flight arrangements, we – ICE, along with the [border patrol] and [DHS] – [are] working really good on the efficiencies of the removal process,” Homan remarked.
He continued: “As soon as we get an order removal, our goal is remove them as quick as possible, regardless of who they are. Get them out quick. Open those beds up for more detainees.”

DHS had quickly publicized Yiannopoulos’s arrest on Thursday at an airport in New Orleans – where he may have travelled to attend a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West, on Friday at the city’s Caesars Superdome.

Officials with DHS touted Yiannopoulos’s arrest on Friday. By Saturday morning, Yiannopoulos’s name was removed from a list of people in ICE detention, and DHS confirmed that he had been deported to the UK on Friday – one day after his arrest.

“He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a DHS release said, adding “The administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport”.
CNN host Dana Bash asked Homan if the rightwing influencer Laura Loomer had, as she claimed, tipped off ICE that Yiannopoulos’s permission to be in the US had expired.
“A lot of people tipped ICE off,” Homan replied. “There are a lot of people who’s calling ICE, and she says she’s one of them. She probably was.
“But bottom line is, it doesn’t matter. He was ordered removed by an immigration judge, and ICE’s job it to execute that order.”
Loomer and Yiannopoulos – who had sanguinely cheered the Trump administration’s deportation efforts before his expulsion from the US – had publicly fallen out.
Homan, meanwhile, denied that the Trump administration had made an example of Yiannopoulos to send a message. “We don’t deport people based on political affiliation,” he said.

articles.title: Nasa launches new space telescope able to see 100 times more than Hubble
articles.summary: The US space agency's telescope is starting a multi-year mission to create a new map of the universe and learn more about dark energy and dark matter.

blocks.text: The successful launch of the telescope took place on Sunday morning local time from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

"What a glorious dawn launch," Jackie Townsend, a project manager on Nasa's Roman telescope, said at the news conference after liftoff. "The ride was magnificent. It put us right where we wanted to be."
About 30 minutes after launch, Roman separated from its SpaceX rocket and is now heading towards its orbiting point around a million miles away.

Astronomer Jenifer Millard said the telescope will be four times further from Earth than the Moon is, where a lot of infrared space cameras - made to pick up what she describes as "heat light"- operate.
She told the BBC this is to make sure infrared light from the Moon and Earth don't interfere with the cameras.

Nasa's James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, also orbits the Sun around one million miles from Earth, but its field of vision is not as expansive. Nasa's Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, orbits at about 300 miles above Earth's surface.
While Roman will look outward into the Universe, Millard said scientists are also anticipating it will find thousands of new worlds in our own galaxy.

Nasa says its "crisp, sweeping surveys will help scientists investigate dark energy and dark matter, discover and characterise exoplanets, map billions of galaxies, study black holes, and explore objects from our own solar system to the edge of the observable Universe."

Dark matter, which is invisible, acts as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the Universe's expansion. Together, they are thought to make up about 95% of the Universe.
"One of our main goals at Nasa is answering the question: are we alone in the Universe?" Fox said at a Sunday morning news conference.

"With Roman, we are going to make this giant leap forward... that is going to allow us to look at these distant, distant worlds and start to really resolve the atmosphere around them to let us know: could they be habitable?"
Millard said, through the work of telescopes like Roman, scientists are hoping to create "enormous cosmic maps" of the Universe at various stages.
"They'll be almost like an onion, so you can peel back layer upon layer... and see how the distribution of galaxies changes through cosmic time," she said.
"What we want to do is use this distribution to try and figure out dark matter and dark energy because we know they exist, we see their effects, but what they are is a real mystery."

articles.title: Prisons ‘one major event from disaster’ after U-turn on early release scheme
articles.summary:
Critics say the move, which will keep PC Harper’s killers in jail, leaves number of prison spaces ‘too close to the bone’

PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain behind bars after a critical…

blocks.text: PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain behind bars after a critical intervention by Andy Burnham, but the move has led to warnings that overcrowded prisons will be left “one major event away from disaster”.
Announcing a U-turn on the early release scheme after weeks of intense pressure, Burnham said he understood “how strongly people feel about this issue”.
The prime minister’s intervention will prevent the early release of offenders guilty of all forms of manslaughter, as well as rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers.
The decision, which affects about 1,400 prisoners, was welcomed by police, victims’ groups and families, including qualified support from Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam.

But critics said the change could undermine progressive prison reforms in England and Wales. They said the steps Burnham outlined to free up space would take longer to bring into force, putting the orderly management of prisons at risk.

Harper was 28 when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire in August 2019. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the vehicle and both 17 at the time, were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter.

blocks.caption: Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were each jailed for 13 years over the killing of PC Harper, had been eligible for early release under the Sentencing Act until Burnham’s intervention.  Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA

blocks.text: Speaking to the BBC, which first reported the government U-turn on Sunday, Burnham said he had “heard” Harper’s family.

“I heard, obviously, what Andrew Harper’s family were saying,” he said. “I mean, who couldn’t? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison.”
Adlam said she was glad and grateful for the change in the new law but felt “a mixed bag of emotions” and campaigning for the change had been traumatic.

“On the one hand we are glad, but we’ve been [put] through the mill and we are only back at where we were to start with,” she told BBC Breakfast. “We’re not making any headway or anything, we are just literally fighting to get back to where we were.”
Harper’s force, Thames Valley police, said the news would be “welcomed by many across policing and our communities”.

Jason Hogg, the chief constable of the force, said: “Today is not about politics. It is about remembering Andrew, recognising the profound impact his death continues to have on those who knew him, the communities he protected and those who serve in policing today.”
Burnham’s 11th-hour intervention will limit the number of places that can be freed up in the prison estate, which ministers have repeatedly warned is on the brink of collapse.

Before the early prison release scheme that had been due to start this week, the prime minister said spaces would be made available by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.
But critics warned neither measure would free up sufficient space in a system that is operating at 98% capacity in England and Wales.

Up to 6,000 prisoners were due to have their sentences cut short under the new law, but government figures suggest the number will now be about 4,600. With the first batch of prisoners due to be released early in October, prison governor representatives said staff would be put under intense pressure.

“The truth is I wanted to go even further,” said Burnham. “But I’ve pushed the system to the very limits of what’s possible without risking the prison system collapsing within months, putting the public at enormous risk.”
Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, said Sunday’s announcement would not bring reassurance to domestic abuse victims.
“Victims and survivors will still be forced to take measures to protect themselves from dangerous abusers because the government and our criminal justice system cannot,” she said.

Sources accused the prime minister of making a “politically easy decision” and warned that multiple governments had failed to deport foreign convicts. Burnham admitted the number that could be returned was in the “hundreds”.
The prime minister’s pledge to “end the injustice” of indefinite jail terms (IPPs) in this parliament was hailed as “a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for”.

But prison experts said it would be complicated, take time and would be unlikely to free up many places in the short term. IPPs were abolished more than a decade ago but still keep more than 2,000 people in England and Wales behind bars.
“The decision to release people on IPPs is extremely welcome, but the government must now deliver it,” said Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League, a penal reform charity.
She said Sunday’s announcement left the prison estate “one major incident away from a disaster”.

“All it will take is something like a serious riot or public disturbance and any capacity will be gone,” she added. “It is just too close to the bone and the government will be left with very little room to manoeuvre.”

She said the move threatened to undermine changes to the Sentencing Act, which were brought forward after a review led by David Gauke, a former justice secretary, and were designed to improve rehabilitation rates as well as freeing up spaces for people coming into the system.

“The Sentencing Act changes were based on deep work over a year from the independent sentencing review, the government and civil servants, with parliamentary scrutiny of the legislation,” said Coomber. “Today’s announcement has undone some of that work.”
Pia Sinha, the chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, said the government should address the number of people on remand awaiting trial, which account for 18% of those in prison.
“If prisons are full they become warehouses – you can’t deliver interventions, self-harm goes up and rehabilitation goes down,” she said.
“The Gauke reforms were not a magic bullet, but they were brave and they were an investment in the future. That progress must not be lost.”

Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, accused Labour of avoiding parliamentary scrutiny of the changes. “The government must delay the scheme, bring forward emergency primary legislation and exclude the worst offenders properly,” he said.

articles.title: Man killed by falling sign at Christian festival named as church pays tribute
articles.summary:
Robert Guanco, 41, a pastor at Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne, described as having ‘touched many lives’

A 41-year-old man

blocks.text: A 41-year-old man who died after a large wooden sign fell at a Christian festival on Friday has been named as Robert Guanco, a pastor at a church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.
A tribute from his church on Sunday described him as a respected pastor who was a “loving husband” and “a devoted and caring father”.
Six other people were injured when the overhead sign fell at the Big Church festival (BCF) near Steyning in West Sussex, including four who were taken to hospital.
Festivalgoers said they rushed to lift the heavy sign, which read “Everything’s Unmissable”, after it was blown over in the wind.

Jesus Living Water church in Eastbourne named Guanco, describing him as “our beloved brother, friend and pastor”, in a GoFundMe to help his family, who it said faced “unimaginable loss” following his death.

It said: “Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love and his service to God will never be forgotten.”

It added: “He was also a good friend, mentor and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life reflected humility, faith, love, compassion and service. Through his ministry, kindness, prayers and encouragement, he touched many lives.
“His passing is deeply felt by everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.”

blocks.caption: Organisers of the Big Church festival said they were ‘heartbroken’ by Guanco’s death. Photograph: Bigchurchfestival

blocks.text: Organisers of the BCF, billed as the UK’s biggest Christian festival, said they were “heartbroken” by Guanco’s death and cancelled the rest of the event.
“We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church festival 2026, in which Pastor Robert Guanco tragically lost his life and others were injured,” they said in a statement.

“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened. Particularly with the family, friends and church of Pastor Guanco as they process the immense grief of his loss.”
They added: “We are working with the police, the Health and Safety Executive and others as they establish the circumstances surrounding the incident,” they added.
The festival opened on Friday and had been due to run until Sunday. The event, which includes worship, music and various performances, first took place in 2009.

The archbishop of Canterbury, Dame Sarah Mullally, said she was “sad and shocked” by the incident. “I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve,” she said. “I pray for those receiving treatment and the healthcare workers looking after them.
“And I pray too for the other festivalgoers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.”
Many people at the festival were first alerted to the tragedy when God TV announced that “due to unforeseen circumstances” the festival live stream had been paused.
Sussex police’s Det Ch Supt Richard McDonagh said: “Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the man who died and all others who have been affected by this tragic incident.”
He urged anyone among the “thousands of people” at the festival on Friday who had information or video footage to come forward.

articles.title: ‘GB News wouldn’t touch him’: Milo Yiannopoulos will struggle to fit in with UK right wing
articles.summary:
‘Alt-right’ agitator and former Trump backer deported from US is said also to be too extreme for Reform

As he arrives back in the UK after being deported from the US by the Trump…

blocks.text: As he arrives back in the UK after being deported from the US by the Trump administration, the far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos may be wondering what lies ahead for him in his native country.
The “alt-right” agitator, 41, made his name in the US by promoting Donald Trump and associating with his allies before the 2016 election.

But now the Trump administration has unceremoniously dumped the former Breitbart News editor back in the UK after he allegedly overstayed his visa. He has also made plenty of disparaging comments about the president, including that he is “firmly off the Trump train”.
Those in the rightwing ecosystem in the UK say Yiannopoulos is now too extreme to find a prominent berth back home.

The commentator started his career at the Daily Telegraph, where he wrote a controversial blog until 2011, when he started his own website, the Kernel. In 2014 he started working for the former Trump adviser Steve Bannon at Breitbart News, before moving to the US and promoting far-right causes.

He left Breitbart after a controversy over a video in which he appeared to condone sexual relations with boys as young as 13. He later said “sloppy editing” and his “British sarcasm, provocation and gallows humour” had created the wrong impression and denied endorsing paedophilia.

Since he left the UK, GB News has become the ascendant broadcast outlet of the right, but he is unlikely to find a place there. A source at the channel said: “We wouldn’t touch him with a barge pole, not in a million years. GBN had a few odd people to start with and we’ve got rid of them.”

blocks.caption: Yiannopoulos after his arrest by federal immigration agents in New Orleans. Photograph: Department of Homeland Security/Reuters

blocks.text: Of the provocative positions that brought him notoriety in the US, the GB News source said: “He won’t make much money out of it here, he appeals entirely to an American audience. It’s a bigger country and you have a bigger pool of fruit loops.”

There is a growing subsection of rightwing provocateurs in the UK who have been deemed too controversial for the main channels but have established niche brands of their own. The journalist Dan Wootton was suspended from GB News after a guest on his show made sexually inappropriate comments about a female journalist, and after leaving he now has his own channel.

The former TalkTV host Mike Graham has also set up his own independent show. He was sacked after the company said he had failed to cooperate with an investigation into a racist post that appeared on one of his social media accounts. Graham said the racist comment had been the result of his account being hacked.

It is understood that Reform UK will not accept him into its ranks. His former colleague at Breitbart, Raheem Kassam, is close to the party’s leader, Nigel Farage, and is in the UK for Reform’s national conference.
Kassam, who is British but now lives in the US, claimed he was kept updated on the deportation of Yiannopoulos, who he accused of making “lurid and false accusations” against him.
He added: “I got word last month that he was about to be deported. On Thursday night, I got a call. As overly dramatic as it may seem. ‘We got him. In Louisiana.’”
The Maga influencer Laura Loomer has claimed to have reported Yiannopoulos to immigration enforcement over his expired visa.

blocks.caption: Laura Loomer (front, centre) celebrates with Yiannopoulos at a congressional primary election night event in West Palm Beach, Florida, in August 2020.  Photograph: Allen Eyestone/AP

blocks.text: One political party that may accept Yiannopoulos is Restore Britain, which is led by Rupert Lowe, a former Reform MP who had a falling-out with Farage.
Restore has accepted a number of characters viewed as too extreme for Reform, including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson.

Yiannopoulos has praised Lowe, calling him “fantastic” and urging those on the UK hard-right to join Restore. He said “the rising generation of young British activists” all “support Restore” and has taunted Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, online, telling him “you’re gonna lose all your votes to Rupert”. The Guardian contacted Lowe to ask whether he would accept Yiannopoulos as a party member or adviser but did not receive a response.
Kassam said: “He’s certain to resurface in Britain shortly. Perhaps as an adviser to Rupert Lowe, or perhaps as a contestant on some third-tier reality TV show.”

Yiannopoulos used to have more political influence; he was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency.

He was deported to the UK on Friday, according to US authorities. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.
In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on Kanye West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working one of the rapper’s companies.
Last year, Yiannopoulos said he was “never going back home” because the UK needed a “mass deportation programme”.
Yiannopoulos was approached for comment.

articles.title: Trump says NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker should face ‘punishment’ from FCC
articles.summary:
Trump’s threat comes after host described success record of candidates whom president had endorsed as ‘mixed’

Donald Trump ⁠on…

blocks.text: Donald Trump ⁠on Sunday said NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker – host of Meet the Press – should face “rebuke or punishment” from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

Preceding Trump’s comments was a live shot by Welker in which she described the success record of political candidates whom president had endorsed as “mixed” on Washington DC’s NBC affiliate prior to the airing of Sunday’s edition of Meet the Press, according to CNN media reporter and commentator Brian Stelter.

The president then took verbal aim at Welker with a social media post deriding her as the “Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of … Meet the Fake Press,” accused her of “purposeful inaccuracy” and warned that she would “be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”.
The post also said that Trump hoped his appointed FCC chair Brendan Carr – and Carr’s colleagues on the commission – “take this Threat to our Country very seriously”.

Once Meet the Press actually started on Sunday, a guest analyst on the show said “the single most important factor in who the Republican nominee will be in [the presidential election of] 2028 will be who Donald Trump endorses”.

Trump is estimated to have made more than 300 endorsements that resulted in the recipient winning. In the election cycle leading up to November’s midterms, 214 of the 218 House candidates he endorsed winning their primaries, including all 24 Republican senate primaries.

Meanwhile, in gubernatorial primaries, five of the 21 candidates he endorsed lost their primaries, among them Mike Lindell – who finished a distant second in Minnesota to state house speaker Lisa Demuth.
The state’s supreme court on Saturday effectively confirmed Lindell’s 11-percentage-point defeat by rejecting his bid for a recount.
“My Endorsements are stronger than ever,” Trump nonetheless maintained in a 23 August social media post. “There has never been anything close!”

When taking aim on Welker on Sunday, he touted recent primary victories by South Carolina US Senate candidate Darline Graham – sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham – and Oklahoma gubernatorial hopeful Mike Mazzei.
He had said days earlier that any of his endorsed candidates who lost were already faced with “impossible” races – but they had earned his support “out of loyalty”.

How much power Trump’s endorsement carries has been a touchy issue for the president. On Friday, HBO Max talkshow host Bill Maher apologized to Trump for claiming that the president is winning “almost none of” his endorsements. Trump had sent Maher statistics making the president’s case that the talkshow host was wrong.

Welker and Trump have a contentious relationship. In June, he walked out of an hour-long interview with the host after being asked, among other unpleasant topics for him, about having pledged “no new wars” during his successful run for a second presidency.
He started war in Iran in late February alongside Israel, and Trump denied guaranteeing there would no wars if he were returned to the Oval Office.
“You’re a one-sided crooked network,” Trump said at the time. “Let’s call it quits because I’ve had enough. Thank you, darling. Have a good time.”
He added: “You ought to straighten out your press. A country can never be great with a dishonest press.”
Trump’s comments on Sunday about Welker were only the latest instance of him or his administration seeking to bring the weight of the FCC down on media outlets with whom he has become cross.

In September 2025, Carr – appointed by Trump – reportedly put pressure on television station groups to pre-empt Jimmy Kimmel’s show as punishment for a comment that the ABC host, a frequent critic of the president, made in the wake of the assassination of conservative influencer Charlie Kirk. Two conservative-friendly broadcast groups, Sinclair and Nexstar, did so. And ABC opted to “indefinitely” pull Kimmel’s show before he ultimately returned to the air a week later.
Trump has also won private settlements from ABC and CBS totaling more than $30m during his second presidency.

Earlier in August, ABC sued the FCC, arguing that it was being illegally targeted by the regulator after being forced to apply early to renew its eight local broadcast licenses. Among Republicans’ complaints about ABC are that its candidates are not given equal airtime on the daytime talkshow The View.

“Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the network said in its lawsuit.
NBC is licensed by the FCC to directly operate 11 local stations. The network did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Involving itself in broadcast outlets’ editorial decisions and constitutionally protected speech is beyond the mandate of the FCC, which was established in 1934.

Stelter on Sunday wrote that the FCC “can’t punish Welker” because it has “limited power … by design”. But Stelter noted that Carr has been “responsive” to Trump in the past – and “it’s reasonable to think NBC will be targeted next”.

articles.title: Headteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in Nepal
articles.summary:
Rajendra Dawadi ordered students to higher ground with moments to spare after receiving warnings from upstream

A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a…

blocks.text: A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.
Rajendra Dawadi decided to halt classes and order children to higher ground after receiving warnings about the scale of the flooding heading their way.

Dawadi, the headteacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot, which has 1,600 pupils, said he had received four warnings from different people within minutes, including one from Betrawati, a town directly upstream.

blocks.caption: Rajendra Dawadi, the headteacher of Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot

blocks.text: This prompted him to take immediate action. “I decided I shouldn’t delay any more,” he told the BBC. “Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day’s classes.”
Dawadi said during the evacuation of the school he saw a hostel building about 100 metres from the river being engulfed by the torrent of flood water.
“If we had made the decision 10 minutes later, all of us, including the students and me, would not be able to speak to you today,” he said.
One student said Dawadi’s decision had saved their lives with moments to spare. Yunisha, 16, told reporters: “I, along with my friends, survived by just 10 seconds.”

She described the children running up a muddy path to escape as water and debris inundated the town. “Within no time, the bazaar was swept away in front of my eyes,” she said. She was reunited with her family three days later.
At least 69 schools have been destroyed or damaged by the floods, affecting nearly 19,000 children, according to the charity Save the Children.
In Dhading, one of the areas worst hit by the floods, a group of schoolchildren survived the disaster when they left their classroom for their lunch break.
Others in the area escaped when teachers told them to quickly evacuate classrooms just before the waters came crashing in.
The mother of one child told the Associated Press that teachers had warned students: “There is a flood and you should leave bags and tiffins. That’s how they managed to survive.”
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. The country said on Sunday 2,502 people, including 592 foreigners, were out of contact. It reported an updated death toll of 781 people.

The disaster, which struck the Nepal-Tibet border region of the Himalayas on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a wall of water and debris cascading downstream, the US Geological Survey said.

Nepal’s foreign minister has called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the Nepali people had disproportionately become “major victims of climate change” despite having contributed a fraction of the planet’s fossil fuel emissions.

articles.title: Fifteen Britons among 261 foreigners missing in China after floods
articles.summary: Total number of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal at 48 as Beijing mobilises more than 2,100 rescue workers

blocks.text: Fifteen British nationals are reported to be missing in China as the search continues for survivors of the devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet.

Nepali and Chinese authorities confirmed an updated death toll of at least 810 on Sunday. More than 3,000 people are believed missing after flash floods brought upon by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas on Wednesday engulfed Gyirong port on the Nepal-China border.

The 15 missing British people are among 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries missing in China, according to figures released by Chinese authorities, bringing the total of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal to 48. The Tibet autonomous region’s government said the total missing there also included 104 Nepalis, 49 people from India, 33 from Latvia and 18 from the US.

Thirty-three British people had already been declared missing on the Nepal side of the border. Some were on a pilgrimage at the time of the flood, including Hemangini Jitendra Patel and Hema Sunil Amin, two sisters who were last seen on the Friendship Bridge on the border.

The figure for missing Americans has been disputed by the US state department, which declared on Sunday that at least 85 US citizens were missing. The department’s spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said getting accurate information from the region had been difficult, “made even more so by the devastation and the remoteness that we see”.

Chinese authorities have said at least 16 people have died on their side of the border. But there are concerns over a possible lack of transparency from the Chinese government, which has prevented footage of the floods from being shared in the countryand may have downplayed the casualties.

Police in Nepal said 794 people had been confirmed to have died there and at least 2,742 injured. Numerous areas remain at risk of fresh flooding and people who have returned to their homes have been told to remain alert and be prepared to evacuate again at short notice.
Rescue efforts have been affected by the threat of landslides and dangerous weather as well as confusion over which side of the border victims had been on when the waters struck.

Chinese state television reported that officials in Beijing, far better resourced than their Nepalese counterparts, had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated more than 220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts.

Equipment and supplies have been airdropped to frontline workers, while Chinese soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing, CCTV said. The Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had already travelled to the region.

Numerous countries have pledged to help Nepal, including the US which has offered $3.6m in humanitarian aid, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households”, on top of $500,000 previously pledged, and Australia, which will donate more than $3m in assistance.
Britain has committed £5m to Nepal and sent a rapid deployment team, which arrived in Kathmandu on Saturday.

A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: “We are working around the clock to support British nationals and their families affected by the devastating floods on the Nepal-China border. We are coordinating closely with the Nepali and Chinese authorities and have deployed consular support staff to the region to ensure British nationals can access support.”

articles.title: Pumping stations fail as flood infrastructure pilfered
articles.summary: Stolen cables, valves and manhole covers are impairing flood control infrastructure in Metro Manila, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon lamented yesterday.

blocks.text: Workers conduct repair works inside the Estero de Sunog Apog Pumping Station in Tondo, Manila on August 18, 2025.
The Philippine STAR / Edd Gumban
MANILA, Philippines — Stolen cables, valves and manhole covers are impairing flood control infrastructure in Metro Manila, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon lamented yesterday.
“Citizens must not steal or vandalize public assets. Stripping one small wire causes catastrophic flooding for thousands of families,” Dizon said.
Personnel of the Philippine Coast Guard have been stationed at the Sunog Apog Pumping Station and other vulnerable drainage facilities across the capital to prevent further sabotage.
At yesterday’s inspection of the Sunog Apog facility in Tondo, Manila, Dizon found that stolen high-voltage cables rendered the pumping station inoperative since Saturday.
Replacement cables were installed, restoring the pumping station’s operation yesterday before dawn.
“We worked tirelessly and spent massive public funds to restore this facility and for several weeks, residents enjoyed zero flooding despite heavy downpours,” Dizon told reporters.
Heavy-duty check valves, crucial for preventing backflow from the swollen Marikina River, were also stolen from the Tumana Pumping Station.
Stolen iron manhole covers along Roxas Boulevard have triggered car accidents.
Perpetrators will be arrested and scrap yards will be inspected, Dizon said.

“Before throwing them in jail, I want to dunk them into floodwaters first so they can feel the suffering our citizens go through just because they chose to strip specialized wiring for copper scrap,” Dizon said.
“I speak with raw frustration because we spent huge public funds and exerted massive effort to restore these facilities, only for thieves to ruin them for a few pesos at a junk shop,” he lamented.

articles.title: Head teacher evacuated 900 children minutes before Nepal floods hit school
articles.summary: Rajendra Dawadi leapt into action after receiving warnings over waters heading towards his school.
articles.byline: Ashok Dahal and Kamal Pariyar, BBC Nepali

blocks.text: At first, many students did not realise how serious the situation was.
Pupil Yunisha Amatya, 16, said she scrambled to safety with her friends just before the flood hit.
"I along with my friends survived by just 10 seconds only," she told the BBC.

"Just before the flood came, we were in the class studying. Teachers had gathered in one place and initially had no idea what had happened. After five minutes teachers came and informed us about the flood and asked us to go home."
She said one student fainted after hearing about the disaster, but many initially underestimated the danger and waited for classmates who were in a maths lesson.
Yunisha and her friends scrambled uphill through an escape route behind the school.

"I could not walk fast, and my friends helped me to climb uphill. We tried our best to be in the safer zones then. We escaped through a narrow ladder from backside of the school. Within no time, the bazaar was swept away in front of my eyes," she says, referring to the local market around the school.

"If there was no grip in my shoes I would have fallen and students and other people were jostling each other to reach the safer area while escaping. The people who choose to escape from another route are apparently swept away."
Students and teachers initially moved a few hundred metres uphill to safety before making their way to a neighbouring village.
With roads cut off and transport disrupted, many remained stranded for two nights before rescue efforts reached them.
The principal and Yunisha, who both live across the river from the school, were eventually airlifted back to their home village.
Meanwhile parents were desperately trying to contact their children and relatives.
Yunisha's mother, Sabina Kumari Shrestha, says she repeatedly tried to call both her daughter and husband, but neither could be reached.
Her husband, Yubaraj Amatya, immediately headed towards the school.
"Soon after the flood news spread, I tried my daughter's number, but she was not reachable, then I was afraid," he said.

"Within a few minutes I rushed toward my daughter's school and Trishuli Bazar was all swept by the flood, then I thought my daughter was no more. I was so horrified, stopped my scooter, there was flooding but I could not think of returning without my daughter."
For nearly an hour, he had no idea whether she was alive and kept calling her without success. Then the phone finally connected and Yunisha answered.
"Finally, my daughter received my call and I couldn't stop myself, broke out... two relatives that were with me also cried and hugged me," he said.
Yunisha appears tearful as she recalls that moment.
"After I had reached the top of the hill, I received a call from my father. He was tearful and I could not speak a word then," she said.
Back home, her family waited anxiously for her return.
"Even my younger daughter couldn't sleep. But I felt so good to see her after three days (Friday), I am so happy and relieved," her mother said.
Yunisha says she is now thinking about what comes next.
"Now I am worried about my further studies," she said.
"If I had to change my school, I would have to miss my old friends and will face difficulties to make new friends. I am sad about my further studies."
Head teacher Dawadi says better warning systems, including sirens and evacuation alerts, could have helped residents respond sooner.
But he believes his decision to act immediately prevented a catastrophe.
"Had I decided to close the school after the period, nothing might be left, only the bell would be ringing at 9:30."

articles.title: Seven killed and 23 missing in boat capsizing off northern Cyprus
articles.summary: A search and rescue operation is under way after a ferry carrying nearly 270 people turns over after leaving port.

blocks.text: Passengers stand on capsized Cyprus ferry ahead of rescue
ByGeorge Wright and Ruth Comerford
At least seven people have died and 23 others are still missing after a passenger boat capsized off northern Cyprus, the head of the Turkish administration there has said.

Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish republic there, said the ferry had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members when it began taking on water after departing the coastal town of Kyrenia.
The ship's captain and seven crew members have been detained as part of an investigation into "how this tragedy occurred", Üstel wrote on social media.
A search and rescue operation to find the passengers still unaccounted for is under way, which Turkish authorities have joined. Turkish media is reporting the death toll has risen to eight.
The privately owned ferry left the left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at 12:30 local time (09:30 GMT), local media reported.
Üstel said the boat had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday, but had been delayed due to poor weather conditions.
He told Turkish media outlet TRT that the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized.
While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he told the outlet.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rescue boats and helicopter around the sinking catamaran close to the port of Kyrenia

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Rescue boats and helicopter around the sinking catamaran close to the port of Kyrenia
Helicopters and coastguard boats have been dispatched to the scene, while ambulances have been stationed on the beach ready to receive rescued passengers.
Üstel wrote on social media that the "priority right now is human life", adding that security forces, rescue teams and health officials were all on the scene.
He added the disaster will be thoroughly investigated and "even the slightest negligence will be uncovered".
"No one will be spared, regardless of who they are, who is found to be at fault or responsible," Üstel said.
Erhan Arikli, the transport minister of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media that 100 passengers had been taken to shore.
Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan sent his condolences to Turkish Cypriots and said efforts to reach those who were still missing "continue uninterrupted".

"Immediately after the accident, we launched extensive search-and-rescue operations in co-operation with the authorities of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus," he said at a military ceremony on Sunday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Several rescue boats have been deployed by the coastguard to rescue passengers

blocks.text: Several rescue boats have been deployed by the coastguard to rescue passengers
The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic.
On Sunday evening, Arikli told TRT the ship had completely sunk.
Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident".
A hotline has been set up to provide passengers' relatives with information. The nationalities of those who were aboard and the status of the injured are unclear.
Local television has broadcast images of the upside-down ferry in the water, with people wearing life vests atop its hull.
The TRNC, which is recognised only by Turkey, controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.

articles.title: ‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal
articles.summary: Precariousness of living in Devighat by the Trishuli River underlined as waters swell again and residents flee to higher ground

blocks.text: The bodies continue to wash up. But the morgues have already run out of room.

Since the deadly floods coursed through the Himalayan valleys of Nepal and Tibet, the numbers of people killed have continued to rise. The bodies have surfaced in their hundreds and continue to be pulled from the thick, tar-like mud that engulfed everything after the flood waters had receded. By Sunday, the death toll stood at 797 in Nepal and Tibet.

Morgues across Nepal are already overflowing. Authorities say they are overwhelmed with the task of trying to identify the dead, many mangled beyond recognition and turning up miles from home. As places to safely store the victims run out, mass burials have begun in the district of Bharatpur.

DNA samples were taken from each body before it was given a tag and a location number, wrapped in a plastic bag and then placed in a shallow grave. The hope, said the police, was that these bodies will eventually be identified by loved ones through DNA and retrieved for proper funeral rites.

In Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, more than 250 bodies have washed up along the riverbanks. But they are in such a disfigured state that only nine have been successfully identified. Many will now be buried, at least temporarily, in the forest on the edge of the city.

blocks.caption: Residents try to salvage belongings from their damaged homes

blocks.text: In a bid to speed up the identification exercise, local officials have adopted a macabre approach of simply asking people to go through pictures of the bodies and look for identifying features: a necklace, a wedding ring, a tattoo, a scar. Photos of those recovered have been placed on to PowerPoint slideshows, for relatives to sit patiently through, and have been uploaded to the Nepal police website. Outside the morgue in the capital, Kathmandu, photographs of the dead inside have been posted on the walls.

Yet with more than 3,000 still reported missing in Nepal and Tibet, there are fears that the numbers of dead may still rise exponentially. Many of the worst-hit areas, where entire villages were wiped clean away by the apocalyptic tidal wave of mud, water and debris, are still inaccessible except by army helicopter. Speaking on Sunday, the foreign secretary, Amrit Bahadur Rai, said the government had requested “more than 1,000 freezer units” for safe storage of the dead.

blocks.caption: People searching for their belongings in their mud-damaged home in Devighat.  Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: Even in areas lower down the river valley that were decimated by the floods but have remained accessible by road, search and rescue teams have struggled to retrieve all those killed and buried in the mud. On Sunday afternoon in Devighat, a sacred town on the Trishuli River that was left in ruins by the floods, police search and rescue teams prepared to pull another victim from the muddy ruins of a house. All that was visible through the thick mud was their feet.

“It is very tough work. We have retrieved 10 bodies from here so far, maybe there will be more,” said Amabadutta Bhatta, a police superintendent working as part of search and rescue in the city. “The floods destroyed the first and second storey of most homes here. When we finally clear all the mud, which may be many months, who knows what we might find.”

Those who survived the floods in Devighat have slowly come back to see the remains of their houses, many which were wiped away altogether. Standing next to the carcass of her house, reduced to a few concrete blocks and twisted metal, Usha Nepali, 49, wept for the home where she had raised her four children and then her three grandchildren.

blocks.caption: People in Devighat salvage what possessions they can from their damaged homes.  Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: “I invested everything to build this house, so now I don’t know where to go and what to do,” said Nepali. “Nothing is left except this cloth on my back. I haven’t even been able to change clothes since the floods. How can we rebuild this house? This land is no longer safe but it’s the only land we have. The river has taken everything.”

The precariousness of living next to the Trishuli River was underlined on Sunday as the fast-moving waters again swelled dangerously high and rescuers urged people to get to higher ground quickly. Many in Devighat were packing up the few items they could find in their homes, never to return.
Jamuna Magar, 36, said her husband’s family had been living in Devighat for generations. She had come here when she got married and described it as “such a beautiful place”.

blocks.caption: Many returned to Devighat to pack up their belongings before leaving, never to return.  Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: In the minutes after they got warning of the flood, she had time to grab her gold but nothing else. As she stood by the ruins of her house, clutching the only thing she had been able to retrieve so far – a plastic vat of vegetable cooking oil – she said she did not see how they could ever live in Devighat again.

“We had experienced flooding before, but we never knew a flood like this could come and take our house,” she said. “Everything we owned was on the ground floor of the house and now it’s all lost. Even our refrigerator washed away. I’m too worried about my life, about my children’s lives to stay here any longer.”
She feared it would take “decades before they can rebuild Devighat again”.

articles.title: NASA launches first telescope named after female scientist
articles.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after NASA's first Chief of Astronomy, will observe black holes, exoplanets and exploding stars.

image.caption: The Nancy Grace Roman Space telescope blasted off on a rocket from Cape Canaveral, FloridaImage: Joe Skipper/REUTERS

blocks.text: NASA has launched a powerful new telescope designed to explore distant planets, exploding stars and black holes while surveying the universe on an unprecedented scale.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after one of the first women to hold a senior leadership position at NASA, was launched aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday.
The telescope is expected to reach its destination, approximately 1.6 million kilometers (about one million miles) from Earth, in approximately one month's time.
The mission has a total budget of more than $4 billion (€3.45 billion). The first images are expected back on Earth in early 2027.
What will the Roman telescope do?
Astronomers will use "Roman" to investigate a wide range of cosmic phenomena, including black holes, exoplanets and exploding stars.

"It's going to find thousands of supernovae, tens of thousands of planets, billions of galaxies and tens of billions of stars," said NASA science mission director Nicky Fox. "It's going to be able to do things that we've never been able to do before with its massive field of view."
Roman operates in a similar way to the Hubble Space Telescope, which was launched in 1990 and is now showing signs of age while operating with reduced capabilities.
However, Roman is designed to survey the sky far more quickly and will be capable of completing in just one month observations which would have taken Hubble a century.
Scientists expect Roman to generate more than 500 terabytes of data every year. By way of comparison, Hubble has collected approximately 400 terabytes of data in over three decades in space.
"Roman's vast reach will allow us to find the weird, the rare and the unusual," senior project scientist Julie McEnery said on Saturday. "We'll redefine what it means to find a needle in a haystack."
How the Webb telescope captures breathtaking images
Who was Nancy Grace Roman?

The James Webb Space Telescope, named after former NASA administrator James Webb, was launched in late 2021 to complement Hubble. Webb observes the universe at different wavelengths, complementing the observations that will be made by Hubble and Roman.

Launching nearly a year ahead of schedule and within budget, Roman is NASA's first space telescope to be named after a woman. Nancy Grace Roman served as NASA's first Chief of Astronomy throughout the 1960s and 1970s, and retired NASA scientist Ed Weiler said the honor was long overdue.
"This is very, very fitting," he said. "I think Nancy would be very proud."

articles.title: Russia says it helped to repel Niger attempted coup
articles.summary: Soldiers tried to attack a key military base early on Saturday morning, authorities say, but were thwarted.

blocks.text: The Alliance of Sahel States - composed of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso - said the attempted coup was "a betrayal by a group of soldiers involved in an attempt at destabilisation".
The authorities have not said how many soldiers were involved in the attempted coup, nor how many casualties there were.
Niger's military ruler, Gen Tiani, who was sworn in as its president last year after he deposed its elected leader, has also not publicly addressed the incident.
The nation's state broadcaster showed footage of several alleged mutineers being arrested by the Presidential Guard.
On Sunday, Niger Press Agency reported that commercial activity was returning to normal, with petrol stations, shops and other businesses reopening.
Supporters of the government gathered at a public square in central Niamey in support of the security forces and Tiani's government.
Air Base 101, the military site attacked on Saturday, is part of the Diori Hamani airport complex.
It hosts Nigerien military aircraft and drones, as well as an Alliance of Sahel States counter-terrorism unit. Russian and Italian forces are also based there, according to news agency Reuters.
Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all military-ruled countries that have cut ties with Western partners and strengthened their co-operation with Russia.
But jihadist violence remains widespread in all three countries, despite the shift in alliances.
For Niger's government, Saturday's mutiny highlights that the military is dealing not only with an external insurgency, but also signs of discontent within its own ranks.
The airbase where the mutiny began had itself been targeted twice by jihadists this year – once by an Islamic State affiliate and later by an al-Qaeda affiliate.
Nigerien authorities say security forces have increased patrols around key sites in Niamey following the attempted takeover, including the main airport entrance and the presidential pavilion.

articles.title: Want to live in history? N.S.'s oldest wooden home offers 'unique opportunity'
articles.summary: Nova Scotia's oldest documented wooden structure, a 318-year-old National Historic Site in Annapolis Royal, is for sale for $495,000. The de Gannes-Cosby House reflects centuries of French and…

image.caption: The building has been occupied by more than 20 families. Now, owner Alyn How is looking for new homeowners. (Stéphanie Blanchet)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

Nova Scotia's oldest documented wooden structure, a 318-year-old National Historic Site in Annapolis Royal, is for sale for $495,000. The de Gannes-Cosby House reflects centuries of French and British rule in the region and has been continuously occupied.
The 318-year-old de Gannes-Cosby House in Annapolis Royal is listed for $495,000
· CBC News
· Posted: Aug 30, 2026 12:25 PM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
Nova Scotia's oldest documented wooden structure, a 318-year-old National Historic Site in Annapolis Royal, is for sale for $495,000.
Located on St. George Street, the de Gannes-Cosby House reflects centuries of French and British rule in the region and has been continuously occupied.
“It's not an easy house to live in. It's difficult to heat and living in a museum is not for everybody,” said Alyn How, who inherited the home and is acting as the real estate agent.
His parents bought the property in 1983, but How says it’s time for someone new to “put their stamp on it.”

items: How this 315-year-old private home in Annapolis Royal became a national historic site

blocks.text: Selling the one-and-a-half-storey house — located at 477 St. George St. — may take time, How said. The property has been on the market for two weeks, drawing early interest but no offers.

“It's not like a condominium in Halifax, it's not like a bungalow in a subdivision,” he said. “It is a unique opportunity and we're going to take our time to make sure that we find the right buyer for it because it is of national significance.”

Between 1605 and 1710, Port-Royal, now known as Annapolis Royal, served as the capital of the French colony of Acadia. As French and British forces fought over the territory, a final British siege captured the capital in 1710.
Today, the house stands as a reminder of nearly 120 years of Acadian settlement. It was originally built for French officer Louis de Gannes de Falaise and funded by King Louis XIV.
After 1727, it housed British officer Alexander Cosby, lieutenant-governor of the fort and town of Annapolis Royal.
“It’s really important for the patrimonial value of the Acadian people,” said André-Carl Vachon, an author and lecturer on Acadian history.
The building retains many of its original structural features, such as post-and-beam framing and wattle-and-daub infill.
Both Vachon and How hope whoever buys the home next will preserve its historic spirit.

articles.title: Cleverly avoids culture war issues in pitch to be next London mayor
articles.summary:
Senior Tory says Khan has ‘lost passion for the job’ and Burnham is ‘very anti-London’ in interview with LBC

James Cleverly has vowed to run a “classically Conservative” campaign to become…

blocks.text: James Cleverly has vowed to run a “classically Conservative” campaign to become the mayor of London, insisting his victory in the capital would be a stepping stone for Kemi Badenoch to become prime minister.

The senior Tory denied he had resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor after a shift to the right under Badenoch’s leadership. However, in a series of interviews on Sunday he avoided speaking about culture wars issues, which have been a focus for the Conservative leader.
“I am going to put forward a classic Conservative case to be the mayor of London, and it’s about enterprise, it’s about opportunity,” the former home and foreign secretary told Times Radio.
“That is a classically Conservative vision, and it will run in parallel to and supportive of Kemi’s plans for the country as a whole.”

If he wins the Conservative nomination, Cleverly is expected to run a more moderate campaign than the party’s last candidate, Susan Hall. She drew criticism for claiming there was a “problem with crime” in the black community and was forced to apologise for liking a tweet in 2020 that had a picture of Enoch Powell captioned: “It’s never too late to get London back.” Hall lost to Labour’s Sadiq Khan in 2024, who won with 43.8% of the vote.

Cleverly, who lost his attempt to lead the Conservatives to Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has moved to the right as support for Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform UK has grown.

Giles Dilnot, the editor of Conservative Home, who has worked closely with Cleverly in the past, denied a rift. He said he thought it unlikely that the MP for Braintree was using his attempt to become mayor as a route to become the next Conservative leader. “There is not a hidden side order of ‘what’s next’ here,” he said.

Asked if Cleverly was likely to seek to put distance between himself and the Tory leader to attract more centre-left voters in the capital, he pointed to the politician’s 2024 speech during the Conservative leadership contest in which he called for his party to be “more normal”.

“Mayoral campaigns are often focused on the person – the personality is that extra 10% rather than just the rosette,” he said. “James is gloriously normal and I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s selling what he is: a normal Londoner who wants the city to succeed.”

blocks.caption: Sadiq Khan stacks shelves in a Sainsbury’s store in Nine Elms, London, with Andy Burnham, the prime minister, and Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images

blocks.text: Prof Tony Travers of the London School of Economics said the restoration of the supplementary vote system in the 2028 London mayoral election – where voters have a preferred first and second choice, with the second choice counted if no one wins more than 50% of the vote – meant Cleverly had to win over voters in the capital whose first choice was the Liberal Democrats.

“The last thing Cleverly would want to do is put off Liberal Democrats, whose party has been the main beneficiaries of the Conservatives’ shift to the right in the south of England,” he said. “I think we are likely to see him adopt a pre-Brexit traditional, centrist Conservative position.”

The entrance of a Conservative big hitter into the May 2028 contest will raise further questions about whether Khan – who was first elected in 2016 – will run for a fourth term, a question he has so far avoided.
after newsletter promotion
A YouGov survey this month found that 56% of people living in the capital thought he should step down and allow a different Labour candidate to stand.

A recent poll for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, found Khan would win a fourth term if he stood despite a surge in support for the Greens. The Savanta survey put Labour on 33%, Reform on 20%, the Conservatives on 18%, the Greens on 14% and the Liberal Democrats on 10%.

If Khan steps out of the running, Dawn Butler, the Labour MP for Brent East, is expected to stand, while others mooted potential candidates in the Labour ranks including Rosena Allin-Khan and David Lammy, the former justice secretary.
Cleverly told LBC he thought Khan had “really lost passion for the job”, adding that as a Londoner he wanted to stand against “very anti-London” Andy Burnham.
“Andy Burnham just doesn’t get it,” he said. “He’s got a war with London, and London needs someone to fight its corner.”

articles.title: British woman killed in stabbing at German railway station
articles.summary: A 27-year-old German man was arrested immediately after the incident in Rosenheim, Bavaria.

blocks.text: A British woman has died after being stabbed at a railway station in southern Germany in the early hours of Sunday morning, police have said.

The 31-year-old woman was attacked at the station in Rosenheim, Bavaria, shortly before 01:00 local time (00:00 BST). She was taken to hospital where she died as a result of "severe" injuries, the Bavarian Police said in a statement.
Officers arrested a 27-year-old German man at the scene immediately after the incident. The background and motive for the attack is under investigation, the statement added.
Police have asked anyone who may have witnessed "an argument or physical altercation" at the station late on Saturday or early on Sunday to contact them.
The suspect, from the Fürstenfeldbruck district, will be brought before magistrates later on Sunday, according to German news agency DPA.
It is unclear whether the two knew each other or what the woman was doing in Bavaria, DPA also reported.
Rosenheim is one of the largest cities in Upper Bavaria and is a busy rail hub for passengers travelling to Austrian cities including Vienna, Salzburg and Innsbruck.
The Rosenheimer Herbstfest - an event similar to the Oktoberfest beer festival - is currently taking place in the area.
Responding to the attack, Rosenheim Mayor Abuzar Erdogan said "there are no indications of a security threat in our city or of any link to our Herbstfest".

"The criminal investigation department is working closely with the public prosecutor's office to investigate the circumstances and motive behind the crime as a matter of urgency," he wrote in a statement.
A Foreign Office spokesperson told the BBC: "We are supporting the family of a British woman who died in Germany [and] are in touch with the local authorities."

articles.title: Power supply pitch for Pax Silica hitting wall of concerns
articles.summary: The Department of Energy (DOE) is selling a grand vision for Pax Silica’s embedded power supply, but so far, the plan looks more like a back-of-the-envelope sketch than a serious policy roadmap:…

blocks.text: The Department of Energy (DOE) is selling a grand vision for Pax Silica’s embedded power supply, but so far, the plan looks more like a back-of-the-envelope sketch than a serious policy roadmap: heavy on promises, painfully lacking in details, and generating far more questions than definitive boosts to investor confidence.
The bigger question: can current DOE leadership be trusted to deliver reliable power for such a massive undertaking when its own energy planning appears to be stumbling in the dark?

Case in point: the Visayas grid has been flirting with yellow and red alerts for roughly four months, yet the DOE seems content to watch the warning lights flash without reaching for the emergency brake. It hasn’t even decisively explored the Interruptible Load Program (ILP)—the very mechanism that helped keep Luzon afloat when supply tightened. Instead, the DOE points to “sufficient capacity additions” stretching out to 2040. Try telling that to businesses and consumers staring down a power crunch today. You cannot keep the lights on with capacity that exists only in a 2040 spreadsheet; the grid needs megawatts now, not promises for a distant future.

This brings us to the billion-dollar dilemma for Pax Silica: what technology will actually power this mammoth manufacturing hub? By design, the Philippine power sector is technology-neutral. However, current government policy is clearly tilting the playing field toward renewables, while the coal moratorium has effectively slammed the door on new projects.

For a mega-development of Pax Silica’s scale, this is no academic exercise. You cannot build a world-class manufacturing complex on an energy strategy that still cannot decide what kind of power it wants—or, more importantly, how it will reliably deliver it.
Technology choice matters

For now, the government is throwing around a dizzying menu of possibilities for Pax Silica’s 3,000 MW requirement: renewables, gas, and even nuclear—as if the country can simply order three gigawatts off a menu and have it served on demand.

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin’s initial plan is to issue a Circular. But what will actually be in it? Will it offer the incentives, certainty, and firm commitments needed to persuade power investors to risk billions on Pax Silica? Or will it be just another piece of paper looking for a project?

If renewables are the choice, waste-to-energy is likely too risky and deficient for a mission-critical, 24/7 AI hub. Solar-plus-storage raises an even bigger hurdle: land. Rooftop solar can help, but at three GW, the required footprint could dwarf Pax Silica’s own 1,620-hectare site.

Meralco PowerGen’s 3,500 MW-plus-storage MTerra Solar project serves as a sobering benchmark. That venture required massive land acquisitions across Nueva Ecija and Bulacan just to secure roughly 850 MW of mid-merit capacity—not firm 24/7 power. For Pax Silica, the math is brutal: if that much land was needed for far less capacity, how much ground will a three GW AI hub gobble up?

The controversy doesn’t end there. Media reports already cite complaints from local communities near the Pax Silica site alleging forced land acquisition, with claims that landowners were offered as little as ₱300,000 per hectare (₱30 per square meter). If substantiated, the government faces a crisis far more serious than finding megawatts: it must ensure that a flagship economic project does not turn into a land grab where local communities are forced to surrender property at bargain prices so others can cash in.
Wind power isn’t an easy answer either, unless the site boasts a proven, commercially viable resource capable of supporting the scale and baseline reliability Pax Silica demands.

Nuclear is also being floated, specifically Small Modular Reactors (SMRs). But is the Philippines really prepared to put the cart before the horse? Staking Pax Silica’s 24/7 operations on technology whose commercial track record and regulatory maturity are still being tested globally is a massive gamble.

If gas is the bet, the global turbine queue becomes the primary chokepoint. Developers are currently waiting four to five years just to secure equipment, as original equipment manufacturers prioritize the explosive demand from US data centers.
Coal appears ruled out by the government moratorium. But if Pax Silica is deemed strategically important enough to warrant an exemption, is the DOE willing to bend or revisit the policy?

This exposes another critical vulnerability: most Western and Japanese equipment manufacturers have stepped back from supplying coal turbines, leaving Chinese manufacturers as the primary option. That creates an awkward paradox for a US-underpinned project: will the Philippines build a showcase for American investment, only to plug it into a power plant running on Chinese equipment? It would be like raising an American flag over the factory while the power switch says “Made in China.”

Gas faces a similar dilemma. If Chinese manufacturers can deliver gas turbines faster than Western suppliers, will Pax Silica wait years for Western equipment, or rely on Chinese technology at a time when Washington is increasingly sensitive to critical-infrastructure risks linked to Beijing?

Another fundamental question is who will act as the off-taker for the Power Supply Agreement (PSA). Will it be the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), or will the government designate another agency to assume that liability? Whoever signs the PSA carries the long-term financial risk—that cannot be left as an afterthought.

Then comes the make-or-break issue: the electricity tariff. Many industrial buyers, including those sourcing directly through Retail Electricity Suppliers (RES), are paying around ₱7 to ₱10 per kWh. Will Pax Silica have to live with those rates, or can the government drive them down through subsidies and tax mechanisms? More importantly, will those rates be enough to attract power investors—or will developers simply walk away if the yield doesn't clear their return benchmarks?
The battle for investment

At this stage, Pax Silica’s manufacturing hub is not set in stone. If the economic equation fails here, capital will move quickly to wherever the fundamentals are strongest. Investors follow reliable and affordable power, world-class infrastructure, skilled labor, efficient logistics, streamlined permitting, and above all, policy certainty.
Philippine Ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez has already warned that Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia are waiting in the wings to seize the opportunity if the Philippines “drops the ball.”

Vietnam has already built what the Philippines is still trying to prove it can deliver: a deep, export-oriented electronics ecosystem anchored by major global players that is now moving aggressively into semiconductors and AI.

Malaysia is a formidable rival in the semiconductor space, backed by an established network in Assembly, Testing, and Packaging (ATP). Indonesia, meanwhile, is actively flexing its capacity to host power-hungry projects, including hyperscale data centers.

At its core, Pax Silica is part of a US strategic framework to counter China’s dominance over supply chains for AI, semiconductors, and critical minerals. Yet beneath the geopolitics lies a hard economic reality: China’s industrial power costs remain far below what a Philippine manufacturing hub can offer. Strategic alignment may bring investors to the table, but cheap, reliable power is what keeps factories running. No amount of geopolitical goodwill can permanently offset an uncompetitive power bill.

The government may argue that Pax Silica’s power demand will ramp up gradually and that 3,000 MW can be built in phases. But a sequential build-out doesn't eliminate the issue; it only spreads it over time. The pressing concerns remain: which generation technology gets selected, how fast can it be financed and permitted, and will the capacity actually be online when new factory phases open? For an advanced manufacturing hub, "power later" is not a strategy; supply must arrive before the assembly lines do.

If Pax Silica is forced to draw from the main grid while dedicated plants are built, the Luzon grid has little surplus to lend. Its supply is already shared with the Visayas, and its dependable capacity is far too tight to absorb another massive industrial load.

Finally, there is the political clock. With the 2028 elections looming, can investors risk billions on policies that might shift under the next administration? Washington faces its own political countdowns as well. That is billions of dollars riding on two separate ballots—and global capital rarely likes betting on an election-day coin toss.
Industry chatter: With one energy undersecretary retiring this September, who will take on the job of actually firming up the power supply roadmap for Pax Silica?
On another note: Who was that major power company shareholder reportedly denied entry to an online board meeting and left waiting indefinitely in the digital lobby?

articles.title: Nearly 30% of local water utilities curb leaks, losses—LWUA
articles.summary: Nearly 30 percent of local water utilities have curtailed system leaks and commercial losses, offering early momentum to the government’s drive to secure the country’s infrastructure against severe…

blocks.text: Nearly 30 percent of local water utilities have curtailed system leaks and commercial losses, offering early momentum to the government’s drive to secure the country’s infrastructure against severe climate risks.

According to data released by the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), 149 out of 532 regional water districts either reduced their non-revenue water—water that is produced but unbilled due to physical leaks or metering errors—or maintained rates at or below the agency’s acceptable 20 percent limit.
Of those utilities, 87 registered direct operational improvements, while 62 successfully drove their losses below the national benchmark.

The operational gains are especially pronounced in Mindanao, where 61 out of 117 local water districts curbed system losses as of December 2025. Twenty-nine of those utilities managed to push their non-revenue water rates under the 20 percent target.

“Building resilient water systems requires long-term investment, but resilience also means making the most of the water we already have,” LWUA Administrator Jose Moises Salonga said during the Philippine Association of Water Districts Convention in Pasay City.

“By helping local water districts reduce losses, strengthen their operations, and improve their financial capacity, we help them provide more reliable services to the communities they serve,” he added.
Controlling physical and commercial losses is becoming a central economic imperative for the Philippines, where climate disruptions like El Niño frequently threaten raw supply.
Lower loss rates allow utilities to maximize existing production capacity without resorting to immediate, capital-intensive raw source development.

To support system upgrades, LWUA has extended ₱31.74 billion in loans to local water districts since 2022. The funding covers raw water source development, network expansion, leak mitigation, and disaster rehabilitation.

The impact of sustained interventions is visible in operational turnarounds across regional hubs. The Carcar Water District in Cebu saw its audited average non-revenue water fall from 18 percent in 2022 to 15 percent in 2024, beating the national threshold by 3.07 percentage points.
Utilities achieved these gains by pairing continuous monitoring with targeted interventions, including systematic meter replacements, pressure management, and aggressive leak detection.

articles.title: DOE seeks 5 gigawatts from idle coal plants to avert outages
articles.summary: The Department of Energy (DOE) is drafting a policy to compel power developers to either build stalled coal plants or surrender their permits, part of an effort to unlock as much as five gigawatts of…

blocks.text: The Department of Energy (DOE) is drafting a policy to compel power developers to either build stalled coal plants or surrender their permits, part of an effort to unlock as much as five gigawatts of delayed generation capacity.
Energy Undersecretary Rowena Guevara said the directive targets projects that received exemptions from a 2020 moratorium on new coal-fired power infrastructure but have failed to break ground.

By establishing strict work plans and binding execution schedules, Guevara said the DOE aims to force firms to proceed with construction or officially abandon their projects to make room for alternative generation capacity.

She explained that the measure would address a key weakness in energy governance: while renewable energy contracts include clear milestones and automatic termination clauses for non-compliance, fossil fuel developments have operated without similar enforcement mechanisms.

“You can see our existing coal plants break down, some are derated, they won’t be able to produce 100 percent,” Guevara told reporters last week. “Because of this, we need to build those that are not covered by the moratorium… They’re not covered by it, but they are not building,” she added.
The country is currently facing urgent supply buffer challenge as aging coal stations suffer frequent unscheduled outages, squeezing reserve margins in the main Luzon grid.
The DOE originally intended to issue the guidelines in June, though officials postponed the rollout to conduct further industry consultations.

The impending policy will not lift or weaken the 2020 coal ban. Instead, it tightens oversight on the handful of pre-approved or legacy expansion assets deemed critical for short-term grid reliability while the country transitions toward its long-term climate targets.
“We have to fulfill our Nationally Determined Contributions, we have to fulfill our renewable energy targets,” Guevara said. “At the end of the day, we cannot have sudden brownouts.”

Philippines power producers face mounting pressure to deliver on promised infrastructure investments as expanding industrial demand outpaces the deployment of stable baseload power, threatening the domestic economic outlook.

articles.title: First Gen secures renewable supply contract for Alliance Global facilities
articles.summary: Lopez-led First Gen Corp. signed a deal to supply over 25 megawatts of geothermal energy to facilities owned by billionaire Andrew Tan’s Alliance Global Group Inc. (AGI). Under the agreement, First…

blocks.text: Megaworld Global Offices Head Francisco D. Roxas (second from left) and First Gen Chief Customer Engagement Officer Carlos Lorenzo Vega (third from left) lead a switch-on ceremony to mark the transition to renewable energy of key properties and facilities in Metro Manila, Iloilo and Davao of diversified conglomerate Alliance Global Group, Inc., Megaworld’s parent firm. Also in photo are Maria Christina Tangonan (left), Megaworld senior leasing manager; and Maychelle Soriano, First Gen lead customer progress partner.
