articles.title: At least 37 dead and hundreds evacuated after strike on Kyiv weapons depot
articles.summary: An investigation has begun into the storage of weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area.

blocks.text: Thirty-seven people have died and almost 400 have been evacuated after a Russian drone strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area on the outskirts of Kyiv.

The strike caused shells, mines and drones to detonate late on Friday, triggering a blast that damaged nearby properties including a care home for the elderly and disabled, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
He said the storage site "definitely shouldn't have been there" and that an investigation had been launched into "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosive right next to people".
The attack is the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv in recent months, prompting renewed anger.
Four children are among the 42 people injured in Friday night's explosion, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko, with a rescue operation ongoing at the site, in the Bucha district, on Saturday.

Russia's Ministry of Defence said in a statement that its forces had targeted "an ammunition depot" in Myla, a village to the west of the Ukrainian capital, holding "components and launch boosters for FP-1/FP-2 long-range unmanned aerial vehicles".
"Everything is completely damaged," local resident Liubov Pavlenko, 45, told the BBC after inspecting her home.
"There are cracks all around the entire perimeter, and cracks around the windows. Basically, the structural integrity has been compromised."
Zelensky said the decision to store explosives in the village was "absolutely unacceptable", adding: "Criminal proceedings have been opened on charges of official negligence."
The office of Ukraine's prosecutor general earlier said it was reviewing the "legality of the placement and storage of explosive objects and materials" near residential buildings in Myla.
It said the "actions of officials who made the relevant decisions" would also be investigated.
However, Zelensky earlier stated that "there are regulations in place - ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas", adding "appropriate conclusions will certainly be drawn".
He referenced the strike on an ammunition warehouse in Vyshneve in July, which caused a secondary detonation that killed nine, injured dozens more and damaged more than 280 homes.
Friday night's explosion has raised fresh questions about why munitions were being stored so close to people's homes, especially given the regularity of Russian aerial attacks.
"The authorities, the Ministry of Defence - why was this allowed at the depots, in a place where there used to be food?" Borys Daniyluk, 61, said.
"Why were ammunition and weapons stored there, next to a populated village? There are no words, just emotions."
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a "lesson" had not been learned following the explosion in Vyshneve.
The investigation into that incident revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company that had not complied with regulations regarding storage of explosives near residential buildings.
Zelensky indicated that the Myla depot had been operated by Ukraine's armed forces.
"In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence," Koretsky said on Telegram.
"Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again."

Meanwhile, Tkachenko said a 14-year-old was killed in a separate attack in the Boryspil district, while Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said a two-year-old had died after a Russian drone crashed in Obolonskyi.

He added that five people, including an 18-year-old girl, were injured in fresh strikes on the capital on Saturday morning. Five people have been killed across the country over the past day, according to local officials.
Zelensky reported further overnight strikes in Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia, as the Ukrainian army said it had shot down 233 Russian drones.
Russia and Ukraine have been intensifying their aerial attacks in recent months, with Kyiv focusing its operations on Russian economic targets.

Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies.

articles.title: Number of missing in Nepal and Tibet rises to nearly 3,000 as operations continue
articles.summary: Nepal requests foreign ⁠help in identification and storing of bodies, DNA testing and rescuing people from tunnels

blocks.text: The number of people killed in the floods in Nepal has risen to at least 675, the country’s disaster authority has said.

Seven have also been confirmed dead in Tibet by Chinese state media, taking the total killed when a glacial collapse unleashed a deadly torrent through river systems in the Himalayan mountains to 682.

Seven bodies have also been recovered in India from rivers flowing from Nepal and are believed to be flood victims. The number of people missing in Nepal and Tibet was revised up to nearly 3,000 on Saturday.

blocks.caption: People put up posters of missing family members at a hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: The missing list includes 517 foreigners and 933 workers on hydropower projects on the river where the torrent smashed down, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.
A number of rescue workers are also missing, including 45 Nepali army soldiers and 40 police officers.
When a Chinese rescue team reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time on Friday, they found “nothing but ruins”.
Surveillance camera footage from the complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only ⁠on Friday were rescuers able to reach the area.

blocks.caption: The glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal, before and after its collapse. Composite: Planet Labs/AFP via Getty

blocks.text: Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign ⁠help in specialised and technical areas, but not in search and rescue. On ⁠Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage ​the rescue ​efforts on its own for ​now and declined foreign involvement.

The areas in which Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing, rescuing people stuck in tunnels, and storing bodies for longer durations, the foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said late on Friday.

blocks.caption: People search lists for the names of relatives rescued from cut-off areas after the flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Dar Yasin/AP

blocks.text: Khanal said ​there was no ​need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
Nepal has requested that its neighbours, India and ​China, provide bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges have been destroyed.
So far, India has sent three flights carrying about 60 tons of relief material to Nepal, including blankets, medicines, food and water purification tablets, ⁠and a specialised tunnel rescue team.

blocks.caption: An aerial photo shows houses along the Trishuli River destroyed by the floods. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty

blocks.text: China has also dispatched five tunnel experts from Tibet to Nepal for flood-related rescue work, Chinese state media reported, as the country called for emergency aid to be sent to disaster-hit areas and for international rescue cooperation.

blocks.caption: Nepali army personnel rescue survivors from a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPA

blocks.text: Rescuers – including army personnel and police – have been clawing through mud and using drilling equipment to reach more than 100 people trapped inside a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa. More than 350 people have already been evacuated from the site under “extremely risky” conditions and the office of Nepal’s prime minister said the rescue effort had become “extremely challenging” due to adverse weather.
Search and rescue operations were temporarily halted because of rain and fog but resumed on Saturday afternoon after the weather improved.

Kawan Koirala, a rescue worker from the Nepal Scout Disaster Response Team, said they had been struggling in thick, leg-sucking mud. “People want their family member’s body back, either dead or alive, but we cannot find them … you can see the mud,” he told Agence France-Presse, exhausted after an 18-hour shift.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.

blocks.caption: A woman salvages usable materials from her house deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: AFP/Getty

blocks.text: China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geohazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be ‌unstable and that more than 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.

In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.

China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of ​the highest national priority.

In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events. The BBC and New York Times have reported that videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.

blocks.caption: On the ground in Nepal after deadly flash floods – video

blocks.text: The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s belt and road network linking the country to south Asia, with logistics zones and vehicle parks built there in the past decade.
Nepal’s finance minister, Swarnim Waglé, estimated the country will ⁠need $4-$5bn (£3-£3.7bn) for rebuilding. “This is just an ​estimate. Loss and ⁠damage is ​being assessed,” he ​said.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Some of the bodies being recovered had decomposed beyond recognition and will need to be identified using DNA samples, Nepali officials have said.

articles.title: Ombudsman questions bail grants to graft convicts
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday questioned the granting of bail to some accused in graft cases before the Sandiganbayan, calling for convicted individuals to serve their jail terms more…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 10:34pm

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday questioned the granting of bail to some accused in graft cases before the Sandiganbayan, calling for convicted individuals to serve their jail terms more swiftly.

“Sabi ko, marami naman ang nasisintensiyahan. Maraming nasisintensiyahan ang Sandiganbayan pero halos kaunti lang ang nakakulong. Paano? Sinasabi, meron daw tayong presumption of innocence at right to bail,” Remulla said on his radio program.
(Many are being sentenced. The Sandiganbayan sentences many, but only a few end up in jail. How is that? They say there is a presumption of innocence and a right to bail.)

“Pero ‘pag ika’y na-convict na sa lower court, convicted na sa Sandiganbayan, na-convict na ng RTC dito sa graft, dapat iyan kulong ka na. Ang problema, medyo sobrang bait ng korte at hindi ginagawa ‘yung trabaho na ipakulong ‘yung dapat ipinakukulong,” he added.

(But once you have been convicted by the lower court, by the Sandiganbayan, or by the RTC in a graft case, you should already be in jail. The problem is that the courts are being too lenient and are not doing their job of jailing those who should be imprisoned.)
Remulla proposed that bail be set at an amount commensurate with the damage caused by the accused.

“Grant sila nang grant ng bail. Ang bababa pa ng piyansa. Dapat kasi diyan, ‘pag na-convict na ‘yung tao at talagang may petition for bail, ang bail should be set, if ever kung iga-grant mo ‘yan, at the cost of damage na ginawa ng tao.”

(They keep granting bail, and the bail amounts are even low. If a person has been convicted and there is a petition for bail, the bail, if granted, should be set based on the cost of the damage caused by the person.)
Remulla added that bail should be paid through a cash bond rather than a bail bond.
The Ombudsman said his office had requested an inventory of individuals convicted by the Sandiganbayan, including whether they had served time in jail.
Remulla also criticized what he described as the apparent leniency of the judiciary when accused individuals file motions for reconsideration involving bail.

“Basta’t nagkaroon ng motion for reconsideration on a grant of bail, parang walang deadline ang judiciary… May rules sila na dapat sinusunod, hihingi sila permiso, ipapa-extend nila. Pero paano ‘yan, uupuan na lang nila forever? Umaabot ng 15 taon ‘yung kaso, nakaupo lang,” he said.

"Once a motion for reconsideration is filed against a grant of bail, it seems as though there is no deadline for the judiciary. They have rules that must be followed, but they ask for permission and seek extensions.
"What happens then? Are they just going to sit on the case forever? Some cases drag on for as long as 15 years without a resolution.)
GMA News Online has sought comment from the Sandiganbayan and will update this story once a response is received.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Number of missing in Nepal, China floods soars to nearly 3,000
articles.summary: NUWAKOT, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan…

blocks.text: NUWAKOT, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing villages.

The number of missing soared to nearly 3,000 Saturday, according to the latest figures from both countries, with 633 bodies recovered and reports that some of the dead may have been swept downstream as far away as India.

In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list that already included trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
Those who made it out say they have lost everything and now face an agonizing wait to discover the fate of missing loved ones and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away. There is nothing left,” survivor Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP.
Samjhana Thing said she had been waiting three days for news of her missing brother.
“We don’t know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place,” she said.
‘Enormous’ trauma
The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous,” and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise.
Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation meant food and water supplies were running out.
Compounding the search for the missing are fears of further flooding in affected areas.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes to form, and one of these formations has become a direct threat to emergency workers scouring the region for survivors.
Nepali police urged all rescuers to “immediately move to a safe location,” saying they had received information that “a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side.”

In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing suspended its rescue operation in the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding before saying the threat had eased.
State news agency Xinhua reported early Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the area.
‘All swept away’
On the Nepali side of the border, the military located people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched, but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than 100 people trapped in the same area.
Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck.
“The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away,” Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, told AFP.
Nepal reported a death toll of 626 people on Saturday.
There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in Nepal.
Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, seven people died and 554 remain missing, state news agency Xinhua reported early Saturday.
Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.
In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
Pilgrimage route
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.
Sivaranjani Muthunathan was traveling by bus with 56 others toward the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.
“Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told AFP on Friday, showing a phone video she recorded of a torrent surging toward her.
Around them, vehicles were swept away or buried under mud.
“One by one, we also climbed out through the driver’s side,” then scrambled up a hill, she said. /das

articles.title: Deadly strike on Kyiv warehouse prompts evacuations
articles.summary: Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv after the deadly strike, which authorities said killed more than 30 people.

blocks.text: Nearly 400 people have been evacuated after a Russian strike on a warehouse near Kyiv killed at least 37 people, Ukrainian authorities have said.
Videos showing the moment of a huge explosion and the plumes of smoke that followed have been shared online.
The strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area.
An investigation into the "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosive right next to people" has begun, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports.

articles.title: Prosecution panel not ruling out Lachica as witness in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel is not ruling out the possibility of presenting former Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSPG) commander Colonel Raymund Lachica as a witness in the…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 9:30pm

The House prosecution panel is not ruling out the possibility of presenting former Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSPG) commander Colonel Raymund Lachica as a witness in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, according to former Surigao del Norte congressman Robert Ace Barbers.

Barbers, the designated adviser to the House prosecution panel, said they have yet to call Lachica to testify in connection with the Office of the Vice President’s (OVP) alleged misuse of confidential funds because they do not need his testimony yet.

“Hindi sarado ang aming isipan para ipresenta si Colonel Lachica. Kung naniniwala kami na mayroong kakulangan o kinakailangan pang madagdagan ang evidentiary value or puwedeng sumuporta sa aming allegations, bakit hindi?” Barbers said on Saturday.
(Our minds are not closed to presenting Colonel Lachica. If we believe there is a gap, or we need to add evidentiary value or support our allegations, why not?)
Asked whether the prosecution was concerned that Lachica might take full responsibility for the alleged misuse of the funds, Barbers said they were prepared for such a possibility.

“Kung sakaling 'yan ang kanyang gagawin, it doesn't give us any evidentiary value doon sa allegations namin. Problema niya 'yun. Kung 'yun ang gagawin niya, siya 'yung mananagot sa batas,” Barbers said.
(If he does that, it doesn't give us any evidentiary value for our allegations. That is his problem. If that is what he does, he will be held accountable under the law.)
The defense also listed Lachica as a witness, so the prosecution is prepared to cross-examine him if he takes the stand, Barbers said.
During the August 17 hearing, former OVP Special Disbursing Officer Gina Acosta said that Duterte was the one who asked her to disburse P125 million in confidential funds to Lachica.
On August 25, Lachica expressed his readiness to appear before the Senate impeachment court “to tell the truth, subject to applicable laws and security restrictions.”
Barbers said the prosecution will present four more witnesses in the coming trial days: three officials from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and defense counsel Michael Poa.
Poa is set to be designated as a hostile witness. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Russian attack on Kyiv region kills at least 38
articles.summary: The death toll from a Russian strike on a warehouse west of Kyiv, the war's deadliest attack so far this year, rose to 38 with four people still missing, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said…

image.caption: Firefighters work at the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv on Saturday, as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue. (Oleksandr Gusev/Reuters)

blocks.text: World

The death toll from a Russian strike on a warehouse west of Kyiv, the war's deadliest attack so far this year, rose to 38 with four people still missing, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media Sunday.
Almost constant air raids in Ukrainian capital have now reached their 3rd day

The strike on Friday night on the warehouse — an ammunition storage facility, according to Ukrainian officials — sparked massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings.
Emergency workers continued to extinguish fires and identify and neutralize explosive devices at the site in the village of Myla, Zelenskyy said.
He said 20 people were injured, including two children.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy called the Myla attack "a terrible situation" and a consequence of "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people." He said a probe was underway into how and why the ammunition came to be kept there.
West hasn't given Ukraine enough to win the war: former NORAD commander
Russia vows 'massive strikes' against energy sector

Russia's Defence Ministry said on Sunday it is preparing to launch "massive strikes" against Ukraine's energy infrastructure, following a Ukrainian drone campaign against a retailer dubbed "Russia's Amazon" as well as the country's oil and gas sector, which Kyiv says both funds and directly fuels Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Sunday vowed "an appropriate response" to what he said was Ukraine's "path of escalation" and targeting of Russia's civilian economy.

items: Russian attacks kill at least 20 in Kyiv
Russian missile and drone barrage in Ukrainian capital region kills 17

blocks.text: Ukraine launched deadly strikes in recent months on the facilities of Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, saying the company sells dual-use goods that have aided the Kremlin's war effort. Ukrainian drones have also pounded Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure, prompting an unprecedented fuel crisis in a country that is one of the world's biggest energy producers.
See the aftermath of Russian strikes on warehouses around Kyiv
Ukraine's new defence chief seeks to close funding gap

Ukraine's new defence minister, Yevhen Khmara, said the ministry has options for closing the multibillion-dollar funding gap he inherited from his predecessor, including seeking more contributions from partners.

Khmara made the remarks at his first briefing with reporters since taking the post on Saturday. His appointment followed weeks of protests after Mykhailo Fedorov's dismissal that sparked a military reset in Kyiv and culminated in a video in which Fedorov called for elections. Khmara's comments were released for publication on Sunday.

Khmara, a former special forces officer who left military service to become a civilian minister, takes over as Kyiv's war effort faces mounting financial pressures. He said a priority will be avoiding battlefield shortages while ensuring soldiers are paid and other essential needs are met.
Is Ukraine running out of interceptors? | About That
Kyiv sends hundreds of drones into Russia
Also on Sunday, Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces downed or neutralized almost 500 Ukrainian drones launched overnight.

Independent news channels on Russian and Ukrainian Telegram claimed the drone strikes set fire to a major oil refinery in Kirishi, southeast of St Petersburg. The facility, Kirishi Petroleum Organic Synthesis, is one of Russia's largest oil refineries and the only one in the country's northwest.

There was no immediate confirmation from authorities, but local governor Alexander Drozdenko on Sunday reported that a fire broke out "in Kirishi's industrial zone" following the drone strikes. He said a total of 62 drones had been shot down over the surrounding region.

Russian strikes on Kyiv on Saturday killed a two-year-old girl and injured 12 others, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Sunday. In the village of Bilbasovka in eastern Ukraine, a 13-year-old child and an adult were killed after Russian troops dropped bombs on private houses Sunday, according to local official Vadim Lyakh.

Also on Sunday, a Ukrainian strike on a mine in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine killed a female employee, a Kremlin-installed local official said. According to Leonid Pasechnik, who heads the occupied Luhansk region, five others were injured across the province.
In Russia, Ukrainian drone strikes injured at least four people that same day in the border regions of Kursk and Belgorod, local authorities said.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: DOLE orders contractor of collapsed Pampanga building to pay P11.49M in wages, fines
articles.summary: The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) on Saturday said the contractor behind the collapsed building in Angeles City, Pampanga is liable for P11.49 million in unpaid wages and administrative…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 8:14pm

The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) on Saturday said the contractor behind the collapsed building in Angeles City, Pampanga is liable for P11.49 million in unpaid wages and administrative fines.

In a statement, the DOLE said Golden Years Construction and Steelworks Corporation and building owner Ernest Jackson Lim failed to pay workers’ benefits and committed occupational safety and health (OSH) violations even before the building collapsed.

“The amount includes P1.17 million in unpaid wages during the Work Stoppage Order (WSO), underpaid wages, unpaid rest day premiums and holiday pay, as well as P10.32 million in administrative fines for OSH violations,” the DOLE said.
The decision stemmed from a resolution signed by DOLE Secretary Francis Tolentino on August 17.
The DOLE said the workers’ claims were meritorious, including their entitlement to rest day premiums during the implementation of the work stoppage order from October 16 to 24, 2025.

“A review of the records established several serious OSH violations, including failure to provide personal protective equipment, secure required permits for mechanical lifting equipment, deploy required safety officers and first aiders, and provide temporary accommodation for workers,” the agency said.
The DOLE also found that fake and invalid certificates had been submitted for the project’s first aider and safety officer.
The respondents were ordered to pay the monetary award and administrative fines within 10 days of receiving the resolution.
The nine-story building under construction collapsed before dawn on May 24, killing 30 people. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Habagat rains persist, trigger flooding, evacuations in parts of Luzon
articles.summary: Continuous heavy rains brought by the Southwest Monsoon, or Habagat, caused flooding in several areas in Luzon on Saturday, August 29, 2026.

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 7:42pm
Continuous heavy rains brought by the Southwest Monsoon, or Habagat, caused flooding in several areas in Luzon on Saturday, August 29, 2026.
Pangasinan
In Dagupan City, several roads were submerged in floodwaters. Aside from the continuous rains, authorities also cited the high tide, which peaked at more than three feet, as a contributing factor.
Several residents in Agno evacuated after local authorities advised families living in flood-prone areas to leave their homes.

As of 10:26 a.m., the Agno Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO) reported that the road leading to Cayungnan Road was completely submerged and impassable to all types of vehicles.
Several residents of a barangay in Aguilar also evacuated as authorities reminded communities in flood-prone areas to undertake preemptive evacuations as early as possible.

Barangay Councilor Bryson Ian Soriano shared footage online showing deep, river-like flooding along a road in Barangay Bongalon, Labrador, amid the continuous downpour. Vehicles, particularly light vehicles, were struggling to pass, while floodwaters had entered several homes in the area.

In a social media update, GMA Regional TV reporter Sendee Salvacio reported that some residents of Barangay Talibaew in Calasiao were using makeshift rafts, or balsa, as floodwaters continued to rise.
According to Salvacio, the water level at the Marusay River had surpassed the critical mark. The Calasiao MDRRMO continued to monitor flooded and low-lying areas.
Aside from flooding, a landslide was also reported along a portion of the Macaboboni-Abagatanen Road in Agno. The road was temporarily impassable, and motorists were advised to avoid the area.
Pampanga
Capitol Boulevard in Lelut Baculut, San Fernando City, Pampanga was no longer passable to light vehicles as of 1:40 p.m. due to rising floodwaters. Motorists were advised to exercise extra caution.
Bataan
In Balanga, some residents experienced ankle-deep flooding on Saturday, according to an update from GMA News reporter Bea Pinlac.
Meanwhile, YouScooper Jimmy Mangalindan shared footage showing calf-deep flooding in Balanga City at around 11:30 a.m.
Mangalindan said floodwaters in other parts of the barangay had reached chest level due to an overflowing river.
Bulacan
Flooding also affected a stretch of MacArthur Highway in Marilao, Bulacan, according to GMA News reporter Jamie Santos.
Several commuters were seen hitching rides on trucks to cross the flooded road, while others waded through the water.
Santos also reported deep flooding along MacArthur Highway in Meycauayan, where floodwaters ranged from thigh- to waist-deep.
Tarlac
In Tarlac City, a portion of the Aquino Bridge collapsed at around 11:56 p.m. on Friday, prompting authorities to temporarily close the bridge to motorists.
Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon inspected the bridge, where a section measuring about 60 meters long had collapsed.
The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) said strong river currents caused by the Habagat rains hit the bridge’s foundation, resulting in the collapse. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Raided steel firm possibly being used as entryway for undocumented Chinese nationals --AFP
articles.summary: The steel factories recently raided by authorities were possibly being used as a possible point of entry for Chinese nationals who want to illegally enter and stay in the Philippines, according to…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 7:06pm

The steel factories recently raided by authorities were possibly being used as a possible point of entry for Chinese nationals who want to illegally enter and stay in the Philippines, according to Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Roy Trinidad.
“It is a possible point of entry ng mga undocumented Chinese nationals na pwede kumalat sa area at magkaroon pa ng mas malaking threats sa ating security,” Trinidad said on the Saturday News Forum.
(It is a possible point of entry for undocumented Chinese nationals that could spread in the area and become a major threat to our security.)
Officials recently raided the Sanjia Steel Corp. in Misamis Oriental due to the facility being allegedly substandard.
There, they found 69 Chinese workers, many of whom are undocumented.
The Sanjia firm is one of five steel plants raided by the Presidential Anti-Organized Crime Commission and the National Bureau of Investigation, with the AFP providing additional support.

Trinidad said that Misamis Oriental steel factory was located near a Philippine Veterans Investment Development Corporation Industrial Authority, an Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement site, the 4th Infantry Division of the Philippine Army, and the Laguindingan International Airport.
He likened it to how Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators were placed near critical government infrastructure.
According to Trinidad, around 500 steel plants were closed in China due to their materials being substandard and some of them went to the Philippines.
Authorities are still determining how these steel factories were established in the Philippines in such a short amount of time, Trinidad said.
GMA News Online has reached out to the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines for a comment and will update the story once it responds. Misamis Oriental —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?
articles.summary:
Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took over

In mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by…
articles.byline: Daniela Díaz in Valle del Guamuez and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: In mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southern Colombia where they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers.

They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades.

That was precisely what the former president Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” plan had sought to achieve: negotiating with and disarming all of Colombia’s criminal groups, which are estimated to have nearly 30,000 members.

But the group of just 99 people was the only one to disarm, and did so just three days before the presidential runoff, which was won by the far-right millionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who had campaigned on a promise to end “total peace” and return to a full-on strategy of jailing or killing criminals.

Now, several weeks after the new president took office – and amid efforts to deal with the aftermath of the 7.4-magnitude earthquake, as his government has already begun the promised airstrikes against criminal groups – the 99 do not know what will happen to them.

“We’re in limbo,” said Natalia Bríñez, 29, one of 13 women among the group staying in the temporary location zone, or ZUT by its Spanish initials, a government-controlled zone where, under surveillance and unable to leave, they were supposed to make the transition to civilian life over the following months.

blocks.caption: Natalia Briñez, a former guerrilla fighter, is one of 13 women in the ZUT. Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian

blocks.text: The former guerrillas are housed in beige brick buildings decorated with drawings they painted themselves, including doves of peace, with a communal dining hall where three meals a day are served. No weapons are allowed inside and soldiers guard the ZUT from a perimeter less than a mile away.

One former combatant built a makeshift gym with weights made from metal pipes and tins filled with cement and sand, and there is an improvised football pitch, but most of them spend their days on their phones.

De la Espriella has repeatedly said his government will no longer negotiate peace agreements and has yet to announce what he intends to do regarding the people at the ZUT. The president has not responded to requests for comment.

In theory, any arrest warrants against the group are suspended, and they remain under state protection until 25 December, when Petro’s decree establishing the ZUT expires. But De la Espriella could revoke the decree at any time.

Armando Novoa, the former government official who led peace negotiations with the group, said “the worst-case scenario would be for the new government to close the ZUT, launch a military operation and try to capture or kill them. That would be a crime against humanity, because these people are unarmed.”

Between 2 and 4 August, days before De la Espriella’s inauguration, Novoa led journalists including the Guardian through the ZUT. The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, where he worked, has since been absorbed into the newly created National Security Commission – a move expected to result in more than 200 job losses – and Novoa has resigned.
For now, at least, the ZUT remains in operation and has a small library run by Bríñez, who has a phoenix tattoo on her left shoulder as a symbol of her rebirth away from the armed conflict.

blocks.caption: No weapons are allowed inside the ZUT and soldiers guard it from a perimeter less than a mile away. Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian

blocks.text: “The hardest thing for me has been being away from my children,” said Bríñez, who has a seven-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son and speaks to them on video calls, but will only be able to see them in person once her “transition” is complete, a process that includes vocational training and psychosocial support.
They were also supposed to receive financial support of about £425 a month, which had not yet been paid. In the meantime, some of them were planning to start a chicken-rearing business.

The 99 made up a small part of a group of about 1,000 combatants called Commandos of the Frontier – most of whom remain armed – and are part of the National Coordinator of the Bolivarian Army (CNEB), a former dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) with about 2,500 members which controls the border with Ecuador.

The Petro administration said negotiations were also under way with other members of the CNEB, who published an open letter addressed to De la Espriella saying they were willing to continue talks with him. It is not known whether the president responded.

blocks.caption: One of the works of graffiti in the ZUT painted by the former guerrillas. Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian

blocks.text: The CNEB’s chief “peace negotiator”, Geovany Andrés Rojas, known as “Araña” (Spider), had been in custody since February under a US extradition request for drug trafficking, which Petro had delayed. Last Wednesday, De la Espriella ordered extradition.

Although such groups emerged in the 1960s as leftwing rebels fighting government abuses and seeking revolution – followed soon afterwards by far-right paramilitary groups – ideology has long since been overtaken for most of them by economic interests, above all drug trafficking (Colombia is the world’s largest producer of cocaine) and illegal mining.

“Here in the ZUT, the vast majority were not in the group because of any ideological commitment, but for economic reasons,” said Novoa. “It even surprised us that most of them simply called the group ‘the company’.”

Petro repeatedly tried to negotiate peace agreements with larger groups. The armed factions took advantage of temporary ceasefires to continue expanding, a process that had already begun before he took office. They also clashed among themselves for control of territory and illicit economies, which many security experts say contributed to a rise in homicides, kidnappings and massacres.
“Total peace” was an attempt to address what the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc failed to resolve, as other armed groups and Farc dissidents remained active.

Petro’s administration failed to reduce violence, which instead reached its worst levels in a decade, and to reach the disarmament stage with any of the gangs, apart from the 99 former combatants – who handed over their weapons only on the eve of an election that every poll indicated the government-backed candidate would lose.
“They [the government] told us: ‘If this works, you’re opening the door for other groups and will set an example,’” said Bríñez.
Some security experts saw the agreement as rushed.

blocks.caption: Former guerrillas in the ZUT have little to do and spend much of their time looking at their phones. Photograph: Daniela Díaz/The Guardian

blocks.text: “It was a somewhat irresponsible decision,” said Paula Tobo, a senior researcher at the thinktank Ideas for Peace Foundation, which published an extensive report on why Total Peace failed.

Tobo said the 99 were now in a “legal limbo” because their protection rested on decrees that could be revoked and there is no legal framework for their transition to civilian life. All of the Petro administration’s proposals to regulate surrenders failed in Congress and, under current law, anyone who has committed crimes such as kidnapping or drug trafficking is not eligible for amnesty.

“It’s positive that these people wanted to lay down their arms, but it really wasn’t the right time for the government to take that decision … The previous administration clearly put them at risk of this government suddenly deciding to abolish the ZUT and arrest them,” said Tobo.
The group wrote a letter to De la Espriella reaffirming its “irreversible decision to commit to peace” and inviting him to visit the ZUT. At the time of publication it had received no response.
The youngest member of the group, a 19-year-old who asked to be identified only as Adrián, said they wanted “to have a home, a family”.

However, he knows what he will do if things do not go according to plan. “Honestly, I’d take up arms again, because we’re keeping our side of the bargain and the government should do the same, shouldn’t it?” he said.
Daniela Díaz travelled to Valle del Guamuez at the invitation of the Colombian government’s former Office of the High Commissioner for Peace.

articles.title: Trump gov’t mulls deal to give away part of Yosemite park
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — President Donald Trump’s administration is considering giving away a section of the renowned Yosemite National Park to a private developer. An investigation…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — President Donald Trump’s administration is considering giving away a section of the renowned Yosemite National Park to a private developer.

An investigation published Friday by NOTUS, a news outlet, said the government has spent over a year quietly working to transfer a roughly quarter-mile strip of the park to a company linked through a web of other entities to Nevada-based Kingsbarn Realty Capital.
It is the latest move by the Trump administration to roll back conservation protections of public lands.
In July, the president slashed two Utah national monuments by more than 90 percent, and this month his administration moved to end a rule barring logging and road-building in national forests.

A Kingsbarn-controlled limited liability company purchased an 83-acre plot just outside the park in 2024, and Kingsbarn CEO Jeff Pori wants to build a road connecting the property to one of Yosemite’s thoroughfares — giving the land “exceptionally rare private access,” NOTUS said, citing people familiar with the discussions.
In exchange, the National Park Service would receive land of equal value in another part of California that has yet to be determined.
In a statement to AFP, the Interior Department appeared to confirm that negotiations had taken place but denied any political pressure to reach a predetermined outcome.

“Any land exchange or access proposal involving National Park Service lands would be subject to all applicable federal laws, regulations and Departmental policies, including required environmental review and public notification processes,” the agency said, adding: “No final decisions have been made.”
“If a proposal advances, the Department will follow established procedures to ensure appropriate coordination, transparency and public involvement consistent with federal law.”

Federal election records show Pori has donated frequently to the Republican National Committee and Trump-aligned fundraising committees. Kingsbarn did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Previously rejected by courts
The National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy organization, called the move an unlawful “attack.”

“The Trump administration’s attempts to dismantle America’s conservation legacy are now taking aim at Yosemite with this secretive, backroom deal,” said Mark Rose, the group’s senior Sierra Nevada program manager.
The Yosemite NPS Employees Union said it was “appalled” by the ceding of public lands for private interests, calling the proposed trade “antithetical to what we stand for” as stewards of the park.
There was a previous proposal to develop a road through Yosemite when the 83-acre parcel outside the park had a different owner.
That plan was rejected by the administrations of both Republican George W Bush and Democrat Barack Obama. Courts rejected appeals by the then-owner, Lewis Geyser.

First protected in 1864, Yosemite National Park in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains is internationally acclaimed for its spectacular granite cliffs, glaciers, waterfalls, sequoia trees and wildlife.

Rose said the park was already facing an overcrowding crisis from years of lodging expansion in the area and the Trump administration’s decision this year to scrap a vehicle registration system to limit traffic.
Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California, a fierce critic of Trump, said in a statement: “Yosemite is one of California’s natural wonders, and must be protected from further development.

“The courts struck this project down once, but this administration appears hellbent on moving forward in the face of opposition from the public, Congress and the courts. But the only thing the administration cares about is whether there is money involved. We will fight this again.” /das

articles.title: Cambodia claims online scam hubs wiped out after sweeping crackdown
articles.summary: PHNOM PENH, Cambodia — Cambodia, notorious for being a major center for international online scams, claimed Friday it no longer hosts any of the compounds where the lucrative cybercrime was carried…

blocks.text: PHNOM PENH, Cambodia — Cambodia, notorious for being a major center for international online scams, claimed Friday it no longer hosts any of the compounds where the lucrative cybercrime was carried out, although some remain skeptical.

The government’s Ad-Hoc Commission for Combating Online Scams, CCOS, claimed success for its crackdown at a Thursday meeting with about 50 representatives of foreign diplomatic missions and international organizations led by Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who heads the anti-scam agency, it said in a statement issued Friday.

“This follows the complete eradication of large-scale online scam operations, strict legal actions against perpetrators, networks and involved officials, alongside the systematic establishment of a cybersecurity legal framework,” it said.

Chhay Sinarith’s claims were met with both skepticism and guarded optimism from independent groups that have tracked the scam compounds, which are infamous not only for bilking billions of dollars from people all over the world, but also for carrying out human trafficking.

Thousands of foreign nationals, who are employed to run “romance” and cryptocurrency scams to swindle victims, are often recruited with false job offers and then forced to work in conditions of near-slavery.
Such scams caused estimated combined losses of $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in 2025, said a report in July by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

“The strong confidence placed in the (Cambodian) government’s assertion that all scamming operations in Cambodia have been eradicated is severely misplaced,” Mark Taylor, an independent international anti-trafficking consultant and former head of an anti-trafficking program in Cambodia, told The Associated Press.
“There are credible indicators that significant scamming operations continue and that recruitment of foreign workers into Cambodia for scamming work continues.”
Blue Dragon Children’s Foundation, a Vietnam-based anti-human trafficking organization, took more of a wait-and-see attitude.

“There is no doubt that some of Cambodia’s criminal compounds used for online scamming have closed,” said Michael Brosowski, the group’s founder and strategic director, citing a drastic decrease in calls from people who have been trafficked, although the calls have not stopped.
“We hope that the Cambodian government will keep its commitment to close down these compounds and give greater protection to victims of this crime.”

Chhay Sinarith said that from July 2025 to Aug. 20, 2026, law enforcement forces investigated 793 suspected scam locations and raided 624 sites, while detaining nearly 30,000 suspects representing 39 nationalities.
Cambodian authorities rescued and deported 58,266 foreign nationals, he said, and 3,477 criminal suspects from 29 nationalities were arrested and placed in pretrial detention.

The crackdown was highlighted by the takedown of two alleged kingpins of the illicit trade, Chen Zhi and Li Xiong, influential Chinese businessmen who had also become Cambodian citizens and were extradited earlier this year after their arrests.

Cambodian lawmakers unanimously adopted a new law in March targeting online scam operations with sentences of up to life in prison, following a government pledge to shut down the centers by the end of April.

articles.title: Europe’s monarchs, world leaders mourn Norway’s King Harald
articles.summary: OSLO, Norway — European monarchs and world leaders paid tribute Friday to Norway’s King Harald after the royal palace announced his death at age 89. Harald was the continent’s oldest…

blocks.text: OSLO, Norway — European monarchs and world leaders paid tribute Friday to Norway’s King Harald after the royal palace announced his death at age 89.
Harald was the continent’s oldest reigning monarch. His son, Haakon, automatically succeeded him to the throne.
Here are some of the main tributes:
Britain’s King Charles
Britain’s King Charles III hailed his “dear cousin,” who he said had served “with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility.”

“As Norway mourns the loss of so towering a figure, my whole family join in remembering a much-loved kinsman and friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades,” the king said in a statement personally signed Charles R.
Danish and Swedish monarchs
The kings of Denmark and Sweden called Harald an “extraordinary” leader and good friend who unified his country.
“Both as head of state and a successful athlete, he was an outstanding representative of his country. He gave ‘All for Norway,'” Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf said, referring to Harald’s royal motto.
Denmark’s King Frederik X said the late monarch was “an extraordinary man” who “joined duty and responsibility with presence and compassion.”
Dutch royal family

The Dutch royal family recalled “unforgettable” journeys with King Harald around Oslo and the rest of Norway. “We cherish the memory of our special friendship with him in our hearts. King Harald served his country with love, pride, and conviction,” the family said in a statement.
Belgian royals
Harald’s “humour, humanity and sincerity made him a truly special man,” Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde said.

“Generations of Norwegians grew up with him. For decades, he was a familiar and reassuring presence, a beacon of stability for his country. He fulfilled his role with unwavering dedication, loyalty and dignity,” they said in a statement.
Spain’s royal family
Spain’s royal family hailed King Harald as an “example of responsibility, dignity, simplicity, and tireless dedication to the service” of his country.
“With respect and admiration for him, as well as deep sadness, we offer our condolences” on the king’s death, they wrote on social media.
Jordan’s royal family
Jordan’s Royal Hashemite Court said it mourned the passing of King Harald, “may his soul rest in peace.”
The court “expresses the deepest sympathies of His Majesty and the Jordanian people, as they stand with Norway and its people at this difficult time.”
King Abdullah ordered his court to observe three days of mourning, a statement from the court added.
UN chief
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply saddened” by the king’s death.
“He will be remembered for his engagement for children’s welfare and environmental issues, his support for diversity and calls for generosity,” the statement added.
NATO, EU chiefs
Harald “showed himself to be a dedicated leader,” Mark Rutte, head of the NATO alliance that includes Norway, posted.
“His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO,” he wrote online.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that Harald “served his country with warmth, humility and an unwavering sense of duty.”
French president

Harald “worked tirelessly throughout his reign to strengthen the ties uniting Norway and France,” French President Emmanuel Macron wrote on X, recalling a “warm welcome” on his visit to Oslo in June 2025.
Ukraine’s president
“His Majesty embodied dignity, wisdom, and an unwavering commitment to his country,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a statement.
“Ukraine will always remember his steadfast support and solidarity with the Ukrainian people during the darkest days of Russia’s aggression.”
Canada’s PM
“Canada mourns with you,” said a statement from Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, offering the condolences of his government.
“I had the privilege of meeting his Majesty last March in Oslo, and he spoke of the ties between our nations with great warmth and affection.”
Italy’s PM

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, in a post on X, called Harald “a monarch who served his nation with equanimity, authority and a deep sense of institutional duty, helping to strengthen the ties between Norway and Italy throughout his long reign.”
Israeli president
Israeli President Isaac Herzog hailed the “loyalty and devotion” of Harald, who early in his reign supported the landmark Oslo Accords between Israel and the Palestinians.
Swiss president
Swiss President Guy Parmelin wrote on X that Harald “will be remembered for his steadfast leadership and devoted service to his country.” /das

articles.title: This extremely successful author polarizes German readers
articles.summary: She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced a public backlash.

image.caption: Author Caroline Wahl, shown here at the 2026 German Film Awards, has topped Germany's bestseller listsImage: Sebastian Christoph Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Caroline Wahl, 31, has published three novels to date. All three shot to the top of Germany's fiction bestseller lists.

Now, her fourth book is set to be released on August 28: "1999 Meter über dem Meer" (1999 Meters Above Sea) tells the story of a young woman who takes on a false identity to mingle among the high society in St. Moritz, Switzerland.
It is one of the most anticipated new books of the summer in Germany.
So what is the secret to Caroline Wahl's success?
Debut with a bang
Wahl's breakthrough came with her first novel, in 2023: "22 Bahnen" (22 Lengths) sold more than a million copies in German-language editions.
The story of the young student Tilda, who has to navigate everyday life alongside her alcoholic mother and her little sister, was praised by critics for its straightforward, modern writing style.
What's more, the novel managed to fascinate readers across generations, including references to contemporary pop culture as well as to classic literature.

"The many references make the novels both diverse and ambiguous," said Matthias Schaffrick, a research associate at the Collaborative Research Center "Transformations of the Popular" at the University of Siegen, who recently organized a two-day symposium on Wahl's works.

"What stands out most is how she experiments with different narrative styles and questions them, instead of simply telling a story," Shaffrick told DW. "This opens up a literary space with multiple possibilities, enabling different interpretations and certainly contributing to the appeal of her novels for many readers."
Polarizing ambition

The book's success led to media interest in the young author, and quickly showed that Wahl does not care much for conventions. She speaks her mind freely and doesn't mind facing backlash. "I enjoy being polarizing," she told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper in late August. "I like that there's no gray area, people either hate me, and then they really hate me [...]. Or they like me."

In the podcast "Hotel Matze," she said she wanted to become one of Germany's most famous authors. Her words quickly created a stir, but Wahl didn't mind. "I'm really not up for false modesty. It's not wrong to state your goals ambitiously," she said on the arts and culture TV show "Twist" on the Arte channel. "For young women in particular, it's more extreme than for men — people get irritated when a young woman says, 'I want to be the best.' I want to change that with my attitude."
A passion for fast cars

Part of that is openly speaking about enjoying her newfound wealth. In an interview with SZ-Magazin, Wahl said: "It's not only the writing that is enjoyable, but also being successful. Financial success is also important." She loves fast cars, drives a convertible and bought a camper van she likes to park somewhere with a view of the sea to work.

On social media, Wahl has faced a lot of criticism. She has been accused of making money off the literary depiction of poverty in "22 Bahnen," despite never having lived an impoverished life herself. It's an age-old discussion about whether authors are only allowed to write about things they have experienced themselves. Wahl replied to this criticism on the Deutschlandfunk radio station, explaining that above all, writing to her means "exploring spaces that I don't know and feeling empathy for people who live a different life than mine."

blocks.caption: Wahl is no fan of false modestyImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: But even without the debate on her credibility, a young woman who speaks openly about material success still seems to be unsettling for many people in Germany — men and women alike — as the many negative reactions show. To Wahl herself, the debate is misogynist.

On Instagram, she wrote a caption for a photo of her light blue BMW: "I find it weird and don't quite get why it's cool for rappers or other men to show off their AMGs, etc., but when a woman author wants to buy a sports car (and can afford to do so!!!), people advise her not to do it and more importantly, not to show it in public."
Author and influencer

"What happens when something becomes very popular?" asked literary scholar Schaffrick. "The popularity starts being scrutinized, which you can observe in Caroline Wahl's case. And we can see what it means to be a popular author. It's not only her novels that play a role, but also the persona she creates for herself as an author."

By being active on Instagram, where she has even tested energy drinks, Wahl also taps into the role of an influencer, said Schaffrick. "It makes her even more popular and offers new topics for conversation. At the same time, the public debate shifts the focus away from her literature, which is what's actually interesting about the Caroline Wahl phenomenon."

Wahl herself has admitted that the intensity of the backlash and criticism has hurt her. In an interview with the SWR TV channel, she explained that social criticism is not necessarily her intention. "I'm not trying to change anything with my stories. Above all, I want to tell stories."
'22 Lengths' on school curricula

When it comes to bestsellers, opinions always differ among German literary critics: Is this entertaining literature, or serious literature with high artistic aspirations? The arts and feature sections of numerous newspapers have come to different conclusions on whether Wahl's novels can be classified as part of the latter. In an interview with Spiegel, Wahl said she finds "drawing a line between entertaining and serious simply annoying."

So far, Wahl's novels have not been nominated for the German Book Prize, Germany's highest literature award. In 2024, the writer voiced her disappointment in typical fashion on Instagram: "I'm sad and angry that I have not been included on the longlist, even if I somehow knew this would happen. Too successful, says my agent."
Back then, her debut novel could have been included on the list — a book that was quickly added to school curricula and has now been made into a film.

Likewise, Wahl's novel "Die Assistentin" ("The Assistant") has not been included on this year's longlist. A literature critic from Frankfurter Rundschau had this to say about the decision: "Why is good literature always supposed to hurt before it can be deemed 'valuable'? [...] The fact that an author like Wahl has been ignored, simply because her captivating writing fascinates millions of readers, makes me really angry."
Presumably, Wahl's fans will ensure that her new novel becomes another bestseller — even without the German Book Prize.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Serbia keeps EU, Russia in play ahead of key election
articles.summary: As Serbia heads toward an uncertain election, President Aleksandar Vucic is balancing ties with Russia and EU ambitions. But growing geopolitical tensions and pressure at home are narrowing his room…

image.caption: Aleksandar Vucic is trying to balance Serbia's ties with the EU and RussiaImage: Djordje Kojadinovic/REUTERS

blocks.text: Smoke from the wildfires still hangs over parts of Serbia, but as the flames slowly recede another debate is taking shape in their wake — one that has less to do with firefighting and more with politics.

In early August, wildfires swept across Serbia, burning through more than 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve. Firefighters, soldiers and helicopters battled the flames for days.

blocks.caption: Serbia turned to Russia for help in fighting wildfires in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature ReserveImage: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Then a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 firefighting aircraft arrived in the southern city of Nis. Serbia had turned to Moscow for help, making Russia the first foreign country it asked to provide a firefighting aircraft. Pro-government media greeted its arrival with celebratory coverage, dubbing the aircraft the "Russian beast."

"Considering that there are no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the European Union, the arriving Russian aircraft will significantly strengthen our capacities to fight the fires," said Luka Causic, head of the Serbian Interior Ministry's Department for Emergency Situations.
A pragmatic choice between EU, Russia — or a political signal?
The episode, however, was already being viewed through a geopolitical lens, as Serbia had sought Russian assistance before activating the EU's emergency mechanism.

When it did call on the EU, the response was swift. Brussels mobilized four helicopters from its strategic rescEU reserve, based in Czechia, Romania and Slovakia, along with ground firefighting teams from Germany and Romania.

blocks.caption: Emergency services, including German firefighters, were on hand to help Serbia battle wildfiresImage: Feuerwehr Bonn/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: President Aleksandar Vucic rejected the idea that turning to Russia first was a foreign-policy decision or a sign of Serbia's political alignment with Moscow.

"As far as equipment and resources are concerned, we are a European giant. The helicopters we received from Europe to fight the fires are less capable than ours and have a lower carrying capacity than our own," Vucic said during a visit to the Deliblato Sands.
Zelenskyy in Belgrade
The wildfire episode came less than two weeks after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy made his first official visit to Serbia.

The two presidents reaffirmed their support for each other's territorial integrity, which is particularly significant for Belgrade because Ukraine does not recognize the independence of Kosovo . Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, which Belgrade still does not recognize.
But Vucic is also trying to keep the other side on board, said Vuk Vuksanovic, a political scientist and foreign policy lecturer at King's College London.

Vuksanovic argues that Vucic's engagement with Zelenskyy must therefore be portrayed in Moscow not as a fundamental shift in Serbia's relationship with Russia, but as a response to Western pressure and Serbia's own interests.
"Vucic is now trying to make sure that neither the West nor Russia becomes an open opponent during the election campaign," said Vuksanovic.

"Zelenskyy was primarily received so that the ruling coalition could present itself to Europeans as a great friend of Ukraine. In the same way, Vucic is trying to present himself to the Trump administration as a great friend of Israel, primarily to ensure that neither the European Union nor the United States becomes an opponent of the ruling party during the election campaign," he added.
Vucic's room to maneuver is shrinking
The problem is that the room to maintain these relationships may be shrinking.
The deeper the confrontation between Russia and the West becomes, the harder it is for Serbia to remain close to both without facing pressure to choose.

The European Union increasingly expects candidate countries to align their foreign and security policies with those of the bloc. Serbia's refusal to impose sanctions on Russia remains one of the most visible obstacles to closer alignment.

But Moscow, too, has reasons not to take Belgrade's loyalty for granted, Vuksanovic said. He argued that Russia does not fully trust Vucic, even as Moscow continues to support his narrative about "color revolutions" — a reference to anti-government protests, in this case the student-led protests in Serbia that gathered pace in early 2025. Vucic and Russia have both portrayed the protests as Western-backed attempts to destabilize the government.

For Vucic, however, the longer-term question of Serbia's ties with Russia can wait. The more immediate question is whether he will survive the election, tentatively scheduled for October, and remain in a position to preserve that delicate balance himself.
